title: Axial Displacement of a Steel Tie Rod and Aluminum Spacer Tube Assembly
summary: A context-rich mechanics problem on axial force, deformation of dissimilar materials, compatibility, and total end displacement.
idealizedImageAlt: Instructor reference idealization of a steel tie rod passing through an aluminum spacer tube, with a rigid collar, fixed support, dimensions, and applied tensile load.
problemStatement:
A mechanical engineering team is evaluating a compact tie-rod assembly used in a machine-frame or actuator support system. A steel rod passes through an aluminum spacer tube. A rigid collar attached to the rod bears against the left end of the tube, and the right end of the tube reacts against a fixed support plate.

When a tensile load is applied to the exposed end of the steel rod, the rod elongates while the aluminum tube shortens. Because the free rod end positions or preloads a connected component, the team must determine its net displacement relative to the fixed support.
engineeringGoal: Determine the displacement of the free end C of the steel rod relative to the fixed support at A by accounting for both the elongation of the steel rod and the shortening of the aluminum tube.

variables.label: Length of steel rod segment BC

questions.title: System Function
learningObjectives: Identify the structural roles of the rod and spacer tube.
questions.student: Identify the primary structural function of the steel rod and aluminum tube assembly.
questions.instructor: The steel rod carries the applied tensile load, while the aluminum tube acts as a compression spacer between the rigid collar and the fixed support. Together, they transfer load into the support and control the displacement of the free rod end.
questions.gradingNotes: Students should recognize that this is a multi-member assembly and that both member deformations affect point C.

questions.title: External Load and Supports
learningObjectives: Locate the applied load, restraint, and load-transfer interface.
questions.student: Where is the external load applied, and where is the assembly supported or restrained?
questions.instructor: The tensile load P is applied at the free rod end C. The assembly is supported at A by a rigid plate or wall. The rigid collar at B transfers load from the steel rod into the aluminum tube.

questions.title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace the axial load through the rod, collar, tube, and support.
questions.student: Trace the load path from the applied load to the fixed support.
questions.instructor: The load acts on the steel rod at C. The rod carries it toward the rigid collar at B. The collar bears against the aluminum tube and places the tube in compression. The tube transfers the load to the fixed support at A.
questions.commonMistakes: Do not treat the tube as unloaded merely because the applied force is placed on the rod.

questions.title: Critical Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Identify displacement as the governing response for the supplied data.
questions.student: What is the critical mechanical response to be evaluated in this problem?
questions.instructor: The critical response is the axial displacement of point C relative to the fixed support at A. It depends on the elongation of the steel rod and the shortening of the aluminum tube.
questions.gradingNotes: The base problem is deformation-focused because no material strength allowables are supplied.

questions.title: Relevant Geometry and Material Properties
learningObjectives: Connect the controlling inputs to the axial-deformation equation.
questions.student: Identify the geometric, material, and loading parameters that control the displacement response.
questions.instructor: The controlling inputs are P, LAB, LBC, AAB, dBC or ABC, Eal, and Est. These enter the relation δ = NL/(AE).

questions.title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Convert the physical assembly into a one-dimensional axial model.
questions.student: Before using the reference figure, develop a simplified axial model of the assembly. Clearly identify the aluminum tube, steel rod, rigid collar, fixed support, and applied load.
questions.instructor: A correct model represents two coaxial axial members: aluminum tube AB in compression and steel rod BC in tension, connected through a rigid collar at B, with a fixed support at A and load P at C.
questions.gradingNotes: A clear one-dimensional model is sufficient; students do not need to reproduce the industrial geometry.

questions.title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the axial deformation model.
questions.student: State the assumptions used to convert the real assembly into the simplified mechanics model.
questions.instructor: Typical assumptions are axial loading, a rigid collar, a fixed support at A, linear-elastic materials, small deformations, coaxial rod and tube, uniform member properties, and neglected local effects at threads, contacts, and the support opening.

questions.title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the equilibrium and compatibility steps before calculation.
questions.student: Explain how the displacement of C will be determined from the simplified model.
questions.instructor: Determine the internal axial force in each member; compute rod elongation δC/B; compute tube shortening and interpret it as the displacement of B relative to A; then use δC/A = δB/A + δC/B.

questions.title: Boundary Conditions and Member Action
learningObjectives: Interpret member action from the instructor reference idealization.
questions.student: Using the instructor reference idealization, identify the boundary conditions and state which member is in tension and which member is in compression.
questions.instructor: The support at A is fixed and load P is applied at C. Steel rod BC is in axial tension. Aluminum tube AB is in axial compression because collar B pushes against the tube as the rod is pulled.
questions.commonMistakes: Assign tension or compression from the physical load path, not only from the visual direction of the applied arrow.

questions.title: Internal Axial Forces
learningObjectives: Determine member axial forces and classify their signs.
questions.student: For P = {{P}} {{P_unit}}, determine the internal axial force in steel rod BC and aluminum tube AB. Use tension as positive.
questions.instructor: Equilibrium and the load path give NBC = +{{axial_force_BC_kN}} kN in tension and NAB = {{axial_force_AB_kN}} kN in compression.
questions.gradingNotes: Equivalent sign conventions are acceptable when the physical tension/compression classifications and magnitudes are correct.

questions.title: Steel Rod Elongation
learningObjectives: Calculate rod area and axial elongation with consistent units.
questions.student: Calculate the elongation of steel rod segment BC. First determine its area from dBC = {{d_BC}} {{d_BC_unit}}.
questions.instructor:
ABC = π({{d_BC}} mm)2/4 = {{axial_area_BC_mm2}} mm2. With Est = {{E_st}} GPa = {{axial_E_st_MPa}} N/mm2,

δC/B = NBCLBC/(ABCEst) = {{axial_rod_elongation_mm}} mm to the right.
questions.commonMistakes: Convert kN to N and GPa to N/mm2 when lengths and areas are in millimeters.

questions.title: Aluminum Tube Shortening and Displacement of B
learningObjectives: Calculate compressive shortening and interpret point displacement.
questions.student: Calculate the axial shortening of aluminum tube AB and interpret it as the displacement of point B relative to fixed point A.
questions.instructor:
The tube carries {{P}} kN in compression. Its shortening magnitude is

|δB/A| = |NAB|LAB/(AABEal) = {{axial_tube_shortening_mm}} mm.

Because the tube shortens while A remains fixed, collar point B moves {{axial_tube_shortening_mm}} mm to the right relative to A.
questions.commonMistakes: A negative compressive strain does not mean B moves left. Relate the shortening to the fixed end A and the actual member geometry.

questions.title: Total Displacement of C
learningObjectives: Combine relative member deformations into the displacement of a point.
questions.student: Determine the total displacement of end C relative to fixed support A. Show the displacement-compatibility relation and state the direction.
questions.instructor:
Both contributions move C to the right:

δC/A = δB/A + δC/B = {{axial_tube_shortening_mm}} mm + {{axial_rod_elongation_mm}} mm = {{axial_total_displacement_mm}} mm to the right.
questions.gradingNotes: Require students to show why the deformation magnitudes add instead of relying only on a memorized sign rule.

questions.title: Engineering Interpretation
learningObjectives: Explain the physical meaning and direction of the combined displacement.
questions.student: Explain why the rod elongation and tube shortening contribute to the displacement of C in the same direction. Briefly state what the result means for a component positioned or preloaded by end C.
questions.instructor: The steel rod elongates under tension, moving C to the right relative to B. Simultaneously, the aluminum tube shortens and allows collar B to move right relative to fixed support A. The motions therefore add. For the assigned data, C moves {{axial_total_displacement_mm}} mm to the right, which is the position or preload-setting displacement that the connected component would experience in this idealized elastic model.

title: Bending Stress in a Cantilevered Industrial Operator-Seat Support
studentDocumentTitle: Student Homework Questions - Cantilevered Operator-Seat Support
summary: A cantilever-beam problem integrating load paths, internal shear and moment, hollow rectangular section properties, maximum flexural stress, stress sense, and engineering assessment.
textbookChapters: Flexural deformation of a straight member
idealizedImageAlt: Instructor reference idealization of a cantilevered operator seat with downward load P, offset x, fixed support A, section a-a, and hollow rectangular cross-section dimensions B, H, b, and h.
problemStatement:
An industrial machine uses a side-mounted operator seat so that a technician can remain near a control or inspection station without a support column beneath the seat. A hollow rectangular steel-tube arm projects from the machine frame and carries the downward seat-and-occupant load P.

Evaluate section a-a, located a horizontal distance x from the load line. Model the machine-frame attachment at A as fixed and limit the base analysis to static, linear-elastic beam bending.
engineeringGoal: Determine the maximum normal bending stress at section a-a, identify the extreme fibers in tension and compression, and explain how geometry or load offset could be changed to reduce bending demand.

variables.label: Distance from load line to section a-a

questions.title: Primary Function of the Support Arm
learningObjectives: Identify the primary structural role of the support arm.
questions.student: What is the primary structural function of the hollow rectangular support arm?
questions.instructor: The arm carries the seat and occupant load and transfers that load to the machine frame.

questions.title: Principal External Load
learningObjectives: Identify and idealize the dominant applied load.
questions.student: Where is the principal external load applied, and how should it be idealized?
questions.instructor: The seat and occupant load is represented by a concentrated vertical force P acting downward through the seat-post centerline.

questions.title: Machine-Frame Support Condition
learningObjectives: Describe the fixed-support idealization and its reactions.
questions.student: How should the machine-frame attachment at A be idealized?
questions.instructor: Idealize A as a fixed support that prevents horizontal translation, vertical translation, and rotation. It can therefore supply horizontal and vertical reaction forces and a reaction moment.

questions.title: Dominant Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace the occupant load to the supporting machine frame.
questions.student: Trace the dominant load path from the occupant to the machine frame.
questions.instructor: Occupant → seat → seat post and mounting bracket → cantilever tube arm → fixed attachment at A → machine frame.

questions.title: Why Evaluate Section a-a?
learningObjectives: Explain why the designated section carries bending demand.
questions.student: Why is section a-a an appropriate location for a bending-stress evaluation?
questions.instructor: Section a-a lies in the load path and carries the bending moment produced by the offset load. In a tip-loaded cantilever, the bending-moment magnitude increases toward the fixed support.

questions.title: Governing Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Recognize the expected flexural normal-stress distribution.
questions.student: What mechanical response is the focus of this problem, and what stress distribution should be expected through the tube depth?
questions.instructor: Flexural normal stress is the focus. For elastic bending, normal stress varies linearly through the depth, is zero at the neutral axis, and reaches its largest tensile and compressive magnitudes at the outer fibers.

questions.title: Geometry Governing Bending Resistance
learningObjectives: Relate hollow-section dimensions to bending resistance.
questions.student: Which cross-sectional dimensions most strongly affect bending stress at section a-a?
questions.instructor: The outer height H, outer width B, inner height h, and inner width b determine the second moment of area. Section height is especially influential because the rectangular inertia expression contains a cubic height term.

questions.title: Student-Generated Cantilever Idealization
learningObjectives: Translate the seat assembly into a mechanics model.
questions.gradingNotes: Students should attempt the cantilever model before consulting the instructor reference figure.
questions.commonMistakes: Common omissions are the fixed-end moment, the distance from the load line to section a-a, or the inner tube dimensions.
questions.student: Before using the instructor reference figure, replace the seat assembly with a cantilever-beam model. Show fixed support A, downward load P, distance x from the load line to section a-a, and the hollow rectangular section dimensions.
questions.instructor: A valid model shows a horizontal cantilever fixed at the machine frame, a downward point load P through the seat-post centerline, section a-a located x from that load line, and concentric outer dimensions B by H with inner dimensions b by h.

questions.title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the beam-bending model.
questions.student: State the assumptions used in the simplified mechanics model.
questions.instructor: Assume static loading, a straight prismatic arm, a concentrated load P, linear-elastic material response, small deformation, plane sections, and concentric inner and outer rectangles. Neglect arm and hardware self-weight unless included in P, connection flexibility, local attachment effects, stress concentrations, fatigue, impact, and dynamics.

questions.title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Sequence the equilibrium, section-property, and stress calculations.
questions.student: List the mechanics calculation sequence before substituting numerical values.
questions.instructor: Cut the arm at section a-a and determine internal shear and bending moment; calculate net area and locate the centroidal neutral axis; calculate the second moment of area; set c = H/2; apply |σmax| = |M|c/I; and identify the tensile and compressive extreme fibers.

questions.title: Boundary Condition and Reactions at A
learningObjectives: Identify all reaction resultants admitted at the fixed support.
questions.student: State the boundary condition at A and list the associated reaction resultants.
questions.instructor: A is fixed and can provide horizontal reaction Ax, vertical reaction Ay, and reaction moment MA. For the assigned vertical load, Ay and MA are the nonzero reactions.

questions.title: Internal Shear and Bending Moment
learningObjectives: Use section equilibrium to determine internal resultants.
questions.commonMistakes: Do not use the full distance to fixed support A when the requested cut is section a-a; use the assigned distance x from the load line to the cut.
questions.student: Cut the arm at section a-a and determine the internal shear force V and bending moment M. State your sign convention.
questions.instructor: From equilibrium of the free-end segment, |V| = P = {{seat_V_lb}} lb and |M| = Px = {{seat_M_lbin}} lb·in. Under the common sagging-positive convention, this loading produces a negative or hogging bending moment at the cut.

questions.title: Net Cross-Sectional Area
learningObjectives: Calculate the material area of a hollow rectangular tube.
questions.student: Determine the net cross-sectional area of the hollow rectangular tube.
questions.instructor: A = BH - bh = {{seat_area_in2}} in2.

questions.title: Centroidal Neutral Axis
learningObjectives: Locate the neutral axis using section symmetry.
questions.student: Locate the centroidal neutral axis for bending about the horizontal centroidal axis.
questions.instructor: Because the outer and inner rectangles are concentric and symmetric, the centroid and horizontal neutral axis lie at the section center, halfway through the outer height.

questions.title: Second Moment of Area
learningObjectives: Calculate the second moment of area about the bending axis.
questions.commonMistakes: Use the outer width with the outer height and the inner width with the inner height. The height dimension is cubed.
questions.student: Determine the second moment of area I of section a-a about its horizontal centroidal axis.
questions.instructor: I = (BH3 - bh3)/12 = {{seat_I_in4}} in4.

questions.title: Extreme-Fiber Distance and Section Modulus
learningObjectives: Determine extreme-fiber distance and elastic section modulus.
questions.student: Determine the extreme-fiber distance c and the elastic section modulus S = I/c.
questions.instructor: c = H/2 = {{seat_c_in}} in. Therefore S = I/c = {{seat_S_in3}} in3.

questions.title: Maximum Normal Bending Stress
learningObjectives: Apply the flexure formula with consistent units.
questions.commonMistakes: Use the moment at section a-a, not simply the force. Keep lb, in, and in4 units consistent.
questions.student: Determine the maximum normal bending-stress magnitude at section a-a.
questions.instructor: |σmax| = |M|c/I = {{seat_sigma_max_psi}} psi = {{seat_sigma_max_ksi}} ksi.

questions.title: Tension and Compression Fibers
learningObjectives: Relate bending-moment sense to tensile and compressive stress locations.
questions.student: For the downward seat load, identify the extreme fiber in tension and the extreme fiber in compression. State the bending sign convention used.
questions.instructor: Using sagging moment as positive, the section moment is negative or hogging. The {{seat_tension_fiber}} is in tension and the {{seat_compression_fiber}} is in compression. Their stress magnitudes are equal because the section is symmetric about the neutral axis.

questions.title: Sensitivity to Geometry and Offset
learningObjectives: Compare how geometry and load offset affect bending stress.
questions.student: Which change would most effectively reduce bending stress: increasing outer height H, increasing outer width B, or reducing offset x? Explain the governing trends.
questions.instructor: Increasing section height is generally very effective because the rectangular inertia contains a cubic height term, although the inner dimensions and packaging constraints also matter. Reducing x lowers moment and stress linearly. Increasing B generally increases inertia approximately linearly when the remaining geometry is held comparable.

questions.title: Engineering Assessment and Model Limits
learningObjectives: Explain how to judge acceptability and identify excluded checks.
questions.student: If an allowable normal stress were supplied, explain how you would assess the arm and recommend one modification if it were inadequate. Identify important checks omitted from the base model.
questions.instructor:
{{seat_assessment}}

A complete design must also evaluate attachment and weld stresses, local tube-wall behavior, stress concentrations, fatigue, impact and dynamic occupant loads, stiffness and deflection, connection flexibility, manufacturing quality, and applicable machinery and seating safety requirements.

variants.description: Baseline cantilever idealization, internal loading, hollow-section properties, bending stress, and engineering assessment.

title: Industrial Clevis-Pin Linkage Under Tensile Load
summary: A context-rich mechanics problem on axial normal stress in rods and double-shear stress in a clevis pin.
idealizedImageAlt: Instructor reference idealization for the clevis-pin tensile linkage.
problemStatement:
A mechanical design team is reviewing a clevis-and-pin linkage used in an industrial actuator assembly. The linkage transfers a tensile force between two cylindrical rod members through a forked yoke and a transverse pin. This type of connection is common in hydraulic actuators, lifting mechanisms, automated machinery, and mechanical test fixtures.

Because the connection is part of a load path, the team must verify which components carry axial tension and which connector carries shear. For this introductory Solid Mechanics analysis, the rods are checked using average normal stress, and the pin is checked using average shear stress assuming double shear. More detailed effects such as bearing stress, stress concentration near holes, bending of the pin, contact pressure, fatigue, and manufacturing tolerances are noted as limitations but are not required for the basic calculation.
engineeringGoal: Determine the average normal stress in each rod and the average shear stress in the pin at A. Use the results to identify which idealized component has the largest average stress demand and make a limited mechanics-based recommendation about what additional information would be needed before accepting the connection for service.

questions.title: Primary Function of the Clevis Linkage
learningObjectives: Connect a real mechanical linkage to its structural load-transfer role.
questions.student: What is the primary structural function of the clevis-pin linkage shown in the industry-context image?
questions.instructor: The clevis-pin linkage transfers tensile load between two rod or linkage members through the yoke, pin, and inner member. The joint provides force transfer while allowing the connection to behave like a pinned mechanical linkage.
questions.gradingNotes: Look for load-transfer language: transfer load, carry tension, transmit force, and maintain a mechanical linkage.
questions.commonMistakes: Students may describe the whole machine without identifying the local connection as the load-transfer element.

questions.title: External Tensile Load
learningObjectives: Identify applied loads and their directions from an idealized diagram.
questions.student: Where are the external loads applied in the simplified problem, and what is their direction?
questions.instructor: Equal and opposite tensile loads {{P}} {{P_unit}} are applied at the far ends of the left and right rods. The left load acts outward to the left, and the right load acts outward to the right, placing the connection in axial tension.
questions.gradingNotes: The industry image does not show force arrows; students should use the problem statement and idealized model.

questions.title: Boundary and Connection Idealization
learningObjectives: Distinguish an axial connector model from a fixed-support beam model.
questions.student: For the idealized connection, identify the effective boundary/loading conditions used in the mechanics model.
questions.instructor: This is not a fixed-support beam or frame problem. The surrounding machine members impose an axial tensile load {{P}} {{P_unit}} at each rod end. The clevis and inner member are connected by the pin at A, which transfers load while allowing the joint to be idealized as a pinned connector.
questions.commonMistakes: A common error is inventing wall reactions or treating the clevis body as a support bracket instead of a tensile load-transfer connection.

questions.title: Load Path Through the Connection
learningObjectives: Trace force transfer through a multi-part mechanical connection.
questions.student: Using the component list, trace the load path through the connection from the left rod to the right rod.
questions.instructor: One acceptable load path is left rod → yoke/clevis → pin at A → inner member → right rod. The same path may be stated in reverse. The pin must be included because it transfers load between the forked yoke and the inner member.
questions.gradingNotes: Missing the pin usually indicates the student has not understood the connection mechanism.

questions.title: Critical Components for the Simplified Check
learningObjectives: Identify which components are checked by the simplified mechanics model.
questions.student: Which components or locations are likely to be critical for this simplified analysis?
questions.instructor: The left rod and right rod are critical for average axial normal stress. The pin at A is critical for average shear stress. In a detailed design, the yoke arms and inner member holes may also be critical because of bearing, tear-out, net-section tension, stress concentration, pin bending, and fatigue.

questions.title: Mechanical Response by Component
learningObjectives: Match each component to the stress quantity used in the base analysis.
questions.student: For each critical component, identify the relevant mechanical response or failure mechanism considered in this problem.
questions.instructor: Left rod: average axial normal stress, σ1 = P/A1. Right rod: average axial normal stress, σ2 = P/A2. Pin A: average shear stress, τA = P/(nsAA), with ns = {{n_s}} for double shear. Bearing stress, pin bending, fatigue, and stress concentration are not included in the simplified calculation.
questions.gradingNotes: The double-shear interpretation is the key conceptual point.

questions.title: Relevant Geometric Parameters
learningObjectives: Connect diameter data to cross-sectional area and average stress.
questions.student: Identify the geometric parameters that control the average normal stress in the rods and the average shear stress in the pin.
questions.instructor: The controlling parameters are d1 = {{d_1}} {{d_1_unit}} for A1 = πd12/4, d2 = {{d_2}} {{d_2_unit}} for A2 = πd22/4, and dA = {{d_A}} {{d_A_unit}} for AA = πdA2/4. Because the pin is in double shear, the total resisting shear area is {{n_s}}AA.

questions.title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Translate a physical clevis assembly into a mechanics model.
questions.student: Convert the real clevis-pin linkage into a simplified Mechanics of Materials model. Your sketch should show the left rod, yoke/clevis, inner member, pin at A, right rod, external tensile load P, rod diameters d1 and d2, and pin diameter dA.
questions.instructor: A correct idealization shows two axial rod members connected through a clevis and pin. The external loads P act outward at both rod ends. The left and right rods carry axial tension. The pin at A is represented as a connector in double shear with two shear planes.
questions.gradingNotes: In a student handout, this can be used as an instructor reference or hidden until after students produce their own sketch.

questions.title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions that make the average-stress model valid for a first analysis.
questions.student: State the assumptions used to convert the real mechanical connection into the simplified Solid Mechanics model.
questions.instructor: Reasonable assumptions include static axial loading; circular prismatic rods at the checked sections; concentric load through each rod; average stress is used; the pin is in double shear; the two shear planes share the load equally; friction, bearing stress, stress concentrations, pin bending, thread effects, clearances, wear, and fatigue are neglected.

questions.title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the stress calculation before substituting values.
questions.student: Before calculating, describe the analysis sequence needed to determine the rod normal stresses and pin shear stress.
questions.instructor: Identify the applied tensile load P; compute cross-sectional areas A1 and A2 of the rods; compute pin cross-sectional area AA; recognize that the pin has {{n_s}} shear planes; calculate σ1 = P/A1, σ2 = P/A2, and τA = P/({{n_s}}AA); compare the stress magnitudes and identify the largest calculated average stress.

questions.title: Loading Conditions from the Instructor Diagram
learningObjectives: Use the instructor diagram to define the base mechanics model.
questions.student: From the instructor diagram, identify the loading conditions and the main connection idealization.
questions.instructor: The connection is subjected to equal and opposite axial tensile loads P = {{P}} {{P_unit}} at the two rod ends. The left rod, yoke, pin, inner member, and right rod form a tensile load path. The pin at A is idealized as a connector in double shear.

questions.title: Internal Loads in Rods and Pin Planes
learningObjectives: Determine internal force in tensile members and load per pin shear plane.
questions.student: Identify the internal load carried by each rod and the shear force carried by each pin shear plane.
questions.instructor: Each rod carries axial force P = {{P}} {{P_unit}} = {{clevis_load_N}} N in tension. The pin transmits the same total load between the yoke and the inner member. Since the pin has {{n_s}} shear planes, each shear plane carries V = P/{{n_s}} = {{clevis_shear_plane_load_N}} N.
questions.commonMistakes: Using the full load on each shear plane doubles the correct average pin shear stress.

questions.title: Cross-Sectional Areas
learningObjectives: Calculate circular cross-sectional areas for rods and pin.
questions.student: Calculate the cross-sectional area of the left rod, right rod, and pin using the given diameters.
questions.instructor: A1 = π({{d_1}} mm)2/4 = {{clevis_area_1_mm2}} mm2. A2 = π({{d_2}} mm)2/4 = {{clevis_area_2_mm2}} mm2. AA = π({{d_A}} mm)2/4 = {{clevis_pin_area_mm2}} mm2. For double shear, the total resisting shear area is {{n_s}}AA = {{clevis_pin_total_shear_area_mm2}} mm2.
questions.gradingNotes: Use N and mm units so stress comes out in N/mm2 = MPa.

questions.title: Average Normal Stress in the Left Rod
learningObjectives: Compute average tensile normal stress from axial force and area.
questions.student: Determine the average normal stress in the left rod.
questions.instructor: σ1 = P/A1 = {{clevis_load_N}} N / {{clevis_area_1_mm2}} mm2 = {{clevis_sigma_1_MPa}} MPa. The stress is tensile.

questions.title: Average Normal Stress in the Right Rod
learningObjectives: Compute average tensile normal stress for a second member and compare the effect of diameter.
questions.student: Determine the average normal stress in the right rod.
questions.instructor: σ2 = P/A2 = {{clevis_load_N}} N / {{clevis_area_2_mm2}} mm2 = {{clevis_sigma_2_MPa}} MPa. The stress is tensile. Since the right rod diameter is smaller, it has the larger average normal stress.

questions.title: Pin Shear Idealization
learningObjectives: Explain why the clevis pin is modeled in double shear.
questions.student: Is the pin at A in single shear or double shear? Explain using the clevis geometry.
questions.instructor: The pin is in double shear because the inner member is located between two yoke arms. The load is transferred across two shear planes in the pin, one at each interface between the inner member and a clevis arm.
questions.commonMistakes: If students use single shear, their pin shear stress will be twice the correct double-shear value.

questions.title: Average Shear Stress in Pin A
learningObjectives: Compute average shear stress in a pin with multiple shear planes.
questions.student: Determine the average shear stress in the pin at A.
questions.instructor: τA = P/({{n_s}}AA) = {{clevis_load_N}} N / {{clevis_pin_total_shear_area_mm2}} mm2 = {{clevis_tau_A_MPa}} MPa. Equivalently, each shear plane carries V = {{clevis_shear_plane_load_N}} N, so τA = V/AA.

questions.title: Largest Calculated Average Stress
learningObjectives: Compare average stress magnitudes across different checked components.
questions.student: Among σ1, σ2, and τA, which calculated average stress has the largest magnitude?
questions.instructor: The calculated average stresses are σ1 = {{clevis_sigma_1_MPa}} MPa, σ2 = {{clevis_sigma_2_MPa}} MPa, and τA = {{clevis_tau_A_MPa}} MPa. The largest average stress magnitude is {{clevis_largest_stress_mode}}, with magnitude {{clevis_largest_stress_MPa}} MPa.
questions.gradingNotes: Emphasize that largest stress magnitude does not automatically mean governing failure unless allowable normal and shear strengths are known.

questions.title: Optional Strength Factor of Safety Check
learningObjectives: Use allowable stresses to compute and interpret factors of safety.
questions.student: Using the provided allowable normal stress and allowable pin shear stress, determine the factor of safety for each checked component and identify the governing checked mode.
questions.instructor: FOS1 = σallow/σ1 = {{sigma_allow}} MPa / {{clevis_sigma_1_MPa}} MPa = {{clevis_fos_1}}. FOS2 = σallow/σ2 = {{sigma_allow}} MPa / {{clevis_sigma_2_MPa}} MPa = {{clevis_fos_2}}. FOSA = τallow/τA = {{tau_allow}} MPa / {{clevis_tau_A_MPa}} MPa = {{clevis_fos_pin}}. The smallest factor of safety is {{clevis_governing_fos}}, governed by {{clevis_governing_fos_mode}}.
questions.gradingNotes: For the default allowables, the largest raw stress is in the right rod, but the smallest factor of safety is controlled by the relative allowable stresses. This is a useful distinction.

questions.title: Connector Load and Additional Failure Modes
learningObjectives: Identify what the simplified connector analysis includes and excludes.
questions.student: Identify the connector load carried by the pin and list additional connector failure modes that a detailed design would need to check.
questions.instructor: The total load transferred by the pin is P = {{P}} {{P_unit}}. In the simplified model, this load is shared by {{n_s}} shear planes, so each plane carries {{clevis_shear_plane_load_N}} N. A detailed design could also require checks for bearing stress between the pin and holes, net-section tension of the yoke arms or inner member, tear-out, pin bending, contact pressure, wear, fatigue, and manufacturing tolerances.

questions.title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Make a limited recommendation based on calculated stresses and missing design information.
questions.student: Use the mechanics results to make a limited engineering recommendation. Identify the governing checked stress quantity and state what additional information would be needed to accept the connection for service.
questions.instructor: For the simplified checks, σ1 = {{clevis_sigma_1_MPa}} MPa, σ2 = {{clevis_sigma_2_MPa}} MPa, and τA = {{clevis_tau_A_MPa}} MPa. The largest calculated average stress is {{clevis_largest_stress_mode}}. With the provided allowables, the governing factor of safety is {{clevis_governing_fos}} for {{clevis_governing_fos_mode}}. Before accepting the connection for service, an engineer should also verify material properties, appropriate design factor, bearing, net-section tension, tear-out, pin bending, fatigue if cyclic loading exists, clearances, and manufacturing tolerances.
questions.gradingNotes: A good response does not overclaim safety from average stress alone. It states what has been checked and what still needs verification.

title: Bolt-Group Design for an Industrial Flanged Shaft Coupling
summary: A symbolic and numerical coupling problem comparing solid-shaft torsional stress with direct shear stress in a circular bolt group.
idealizedImageAlt: Instructor reference idealization of two flanged shafts transmitting torque through equally spaced bolts on a circular pattern.
problemStatement:
A reliability engineer is reviewing a rigid flanged coupling between a rotating driver and a pump. Identical bolts on a circular pattern transfer torque between the mating flanges.

The simplified model treats the flanges as rigid and assumes uniform direct shear among the bolts. Bolt preload, frictional torque transfer, bending, bearing, fatigue, and local stress concentrations are excluded.
engineeringGoal: Determine the theoretical bolt count that makes average bolt shear stress no greater than maximum shaft torsional shear stress, select a practical integer bolt pattern, and verify the resulting stress inequality.

questions.title: Primary Function
learningObjectives: Identify the coupling's primary mechanical role.
questions.student: State the primary mechanical function of the flanged coupling.
questions.instructor: The coupling joins two coaxial shafts and transfers torque from the driving shaft to the driven shaft while maintaining rotational continuity.

questions.title: External Loading
learningObjectives: Identify the applied torque pair.
questions.student: Identify the external loading represented in the simplified model.
questions.instructor: Equal and opposite torques of magnitude T act on the two shafts, representing driver input and driven-machine resistance.

questions.title: Torque Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace torque through the coupling.
questions.student: Trace the torque load path from the driving machine to the driven machine.
questions.instructor: The path is driving shaft, first flange, bolt group in shear, second flange, driven shaft, and driven machine.

questions.title: Compared Mechanical Responses
learningObjectives: Identify the two stresses compared by the design criterion.
questions.student: Identify the two mechanical responses compared in this problem.
questions.instructor: The design compares maximum torsional shear stress at the shaft surface with average direct shear stress in each coupling bolt.

questions.title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify variables governing shaft and bolt stress.
questions.student: Identify the geometric and loading variables that govern the two stresses.
questions.instructor: The variables are torque T, shaft radius r, bolt-circle radius R, bolt diameter db, and bolt count n.

questions.title: Load-Sharing Interpretation
learningObjectives: Explain the uniform bolt-force assumption.
questions.student: Under the base idealization, why does each bolt carry the same tangential force?
questions.instructor: The bolts are identical, equally spaced at the same radius, and connected by rigid flanges, so symmetry gives equal tangential force in every bolt.

questions.title: Scope of the Base Problem
learningObjectives: Distinguish the base comparison from full coupling design.
questions.student: Identify important real coupling behaviors excluded from the base model.
questions.instructor: The model excludes preload and frictional torque transfer, bolt bearing, flange flexure, shaft bending, fatigue, fit, alignment, and local stress concentrations.

questions.title: Student-Generated Coupling Idealization
learningObjectives: Create a coupling model before viewing the reference figure.
questions.student: Before using the reference figure, draw two coaxial shafts, mating rigid flanges, n equally spaced bolts at radius R, shaft radius r, bolt diameter db, and applied torques.
questions.instructor: A valid model preserves the coaxial shafts, circular bolt pattern, equal torque magnitude on each side, and all symbolic dimensions needed for shaft and bolt stress.
questions.gradingNotes: A clear 2D or isometric model is acceptable.

questions.title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting uniform bolt-group analysis.
questions.student: State the assumptions used in the base mechanics model.
questions.instructor: Assume solid circular shafts, rigid flanges, identical equally spaced bolts, uniform tangential bolt force, single direct-shear area per bolt, static torque, and neglected preload friction, bending, bearing, fatigue, and stress concentration.

questions.title: Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the symbolic and numerical design sequence.
questions.student: List the calculation sequence needed to determine and verify the bolt count.
questions.instructor: Derive shaft stress; write bolt-group torque equilibrium; derive bolt stress; equate the two stresses; solve for theoretical n; round upward to an allowed pattern; and verify the selected bolt stress.

questions.title: Boundary Conditions and Torque Equilibrium
learningObjectives: Describe steady torque transmission.
questions.student: Describe the boundary/load representation and write the global torque-equilibrium condition.
questions.instructor: The machine sides apply equal and opposite torques. For steady transmission, the shaft and coupling carry constant internal torque magnitude {{coupling_torque_Nmm}} N·mm.

questions.title: Maximum Shaft Shear Stress
learningObjectives: Derive and evaluate maximum shaft shear stress.
questions.student: Derive the maximum torsional shear stress in the solid shaft and evaluate it for the assigned values.
questions.instructor: J = πr4/2 = {{coupling_shaft_J_mm4}} mm4, so τshaft,max = Tr/J = 2T/(πr3) = {{coupling_shaft_tau_MPa}} MPa.

questions.title: Tangential Force in Each Bolt
learningObjectives: Relate total torque to individual bolt force.
questions.student: Assuming uniform load sharing among n bolts at radius R, determine the tangential force carried by each bolt.
questions.instructor: Torque equilibrium gives T = nFbR, so Fb = T/(nR). For the selected pattern, Fb = {{coupling_bolt_force_N}} N.

questions.title: Average Shear Stress in Each Bolt
learningObjectives: Derive average bolt shear stress.
questions.student: Derive the average direct shear stress in each bolt.
questions.instructor: Ab = πdb2/4 = {{coupling_bolt_area_mm2}} mm2. Therefore τb = 4T/(nπR db2).

questions.title: Required Theoretical Bolt Count
learningObjectives: Derive the symbolic minimum bolt count.
questions.student: Set average bolt shear stress equal to maximum shaft shear stress and solve for theoretical bolt count.
questions.instructor: Equating 4T/(nπR db2) and 2T/(πr3) gives nreq = 2r3/(R db2) = {{coupling_n_req}}. Torque and π cancel because both stresses scale linearly with torque.

questions.title: Practical Integer Selection
learningObjectives: Convert theoretical count into an allowed bolt pattern.
questions.student: Select the smallest allowed bolt pattern not less than the theoretical requirement.
questions.instructor: The smallest unrestricted integer is {{coupling_n_integer}} bolts. Applying the assigned pattern increment gives {{coupling_n_selected}} bolts. {{coupling_pattern_assessment}}

questions.title: Selected-Pattern Verification
learningObjectives: Verify the selected bolt pattern against the criterion.
questions.student: Calculate bolt force and bolt shear stress for the selected pattern, then verify the stress inequality.
questions.instructor: Each selected bolt carries {{coupling_bolt_force_N}} N, producing τb = {{coupling_bolt_tau_MPa}} MPa. The ratio τb/τshaft,max is {{coupling_stress_ratio}}. {{coupling_stress_assessment}}

questions.title: Sensitivity and Design Modification
learningObjectives: Interpret parameter sensitivity from the symbolic result.
questions.student: Explain how changing r, R, or db affects required bolt count.
questions.instructor: The requirement scales as n proportional to r3, 1/R, and 1/db2. Increasing bolt-circle radius or bolt diameter reduces required count, while increasing shaft radius raises it strongly under this stress-matching criterion.

questions.title: Engineering Assessment
learningObjectives: Make a bounded bolt-pattern recommendation.
questions.student: Provide a concise mechanics-based recommendation for the bolt pattern and identify omitted design checks.
questions.instructor:
{{coupling_recommendation}}

A complete design must also check bolt bearing and fatigue, flange strength and flexure, preload and friction, shaft-hub details, fit, alignment, stress concentrations, and applicable coupling standards.
questions.gradingNotes: The recommendation must be limited to the stated stress-matching model.

title: Hydraulic Press Punching Shear and Bearing Stress Check
summary: A context-rich mechanics problem on average bearing stress and punching shear stress in a press-loaded plate.
idealizedImageAlt: Instructor idealization showing the press ram, plate, bearing area, and punching shear sections.
problemStatement:
A manufacturing engineering team is evaluating a hydraulic press fixture used to apply a vertical compressive load through a cylindrical ram onto a flat metal plate. The plate is supported by two fixture blocks with an opening beneath the loaded region. This type of setup appears in pressing operations, material testing, tooling qualification, and shop-floor fixtures where concentrated loads are introduced into relatively thin plates.

As a junior mechanical or manufacturing engineer, you must identify how the load is transferred from the ram into the supported plate and determine the average stress quantities that are relevant to the simplified Solid Mechanics model. The analysis focuses on two different average-stress mechanisms: bearing stress under the ram and punching shear stress through the plate along sections AC and BD.
engineeringGoal: Determine the average punching shear stress developed in the plate along sections AC and BD, and determine the average bearing stress on the plate surface under the cylindrical ram. Use these results to identify which simplified stress quantity is larger and state what additional material data would be needed before accepting the fixture for service.

variables.label: Overall plate/support width in idealized view

questions.title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Connect the physical press setup to load transfer
Identify local plate stress concerns
questions.student: What is the primary structural function of the press fixture system?
questions.instructor:
The system transfers a compressive load from a hydraulic press ram into a flat metal plate and then into the support blocks and press table. The plate must resist local contact/bearing stress under the ram and possible punching shear through its thickness.

Students should connect the physical setup to load transfer, not describe the entire press machine in broad terms.

questions.title: External Load
learningObjectives: Identify where the load is applied
Relate the press ram to the idealized load
questions.student: Where is the external load applied, and what is its direction?
questions.instructor:
The external load P is applied vertically downward through the cylindrical ram onto the top surface of the flat plate.

The industry image has no labels; students should use the problem statement and idealized diagram to identify the load.

questions.title: Supports and Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Identify simplified supports
Distinguish local stress checks from beam bending analysis
questions.student: Identify the supports or boundary constraints in the idealized fixture model.
questions.instructor:
The plate is supported from below by two support blocks on either side of the opening. In the simplified model, the supports provide upward reaction forces to the plate while the central region between the supports is unsupported.

This is not a fixed-end beam problem for the base analysis; the focus is average bearing and punching shear.

questions.title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace load from ram to fixture base
Name the contact and shear-transfer regions
questions.student: Using the component list, trace the load path from the press ram to the fixture base.
questions.instructor:
One acceptable load path is: hydraulic ram → bearing contact region on top of the plate → plate material around the loaded region → punching shear sections AC and BD → support blocks → press table/fixture base.

The key point is that the load does not vanish at the plate; it must transfer through contact and shear regions into the supports.

questions.title: Critical Components and Locations
learningObjectives: Identify critical locations for average stress checks
Separate included and excluded components
questions.student: Which components or locations are likely to be critical for this simplified problem?
questions.instructor:
The flat plate is the critical component. The important locations are the contact area directly under the ram and the potential punching shear sections AC and BD through the plate thickness.

Students may mention support blocks, but the base problem provides geometry for the plate stress checks only.

questions.title: Critical Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Distinguish bearing stress from punching shear stress
Identify the relevant stress mechanism at each location
questions.student: For each critical location, identify the relevant mechanical response or failure mechanism considered in this problem.
questions.instructor:
At the top surface under the ram, the relevant response is average bearing/compressive contact stress. Along sections AC and BD, the relevant response is average punching shear stress through the plate thickness.

Bending, contact nonlinearity, local yielding, and plastic deformation are not included in the simplified calculation.

questions.title: Relevant Geometric and Load Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify variables controlling bearing and punching shear
Connect area definitions to stress definitions
questions.student: Identify the geometric and load parameters that control the bearing stress and punching shear stress.
questions.instructor:
The relevant parameters are applied load P, ram diameter d, plate thickness t, support opening distance s, and overall plate/support width b. For the simplified calculations here, bearing stress is controlled by the contact area under the ram, and punching shear is controlled by the shear area through sections AC and BD.

Students should connect area definitions to stress definitions rather than simply listing dimensions.

questions.title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Translate a press setup into an average-stress model
Identify bearing and punching shear surfaces
questions.student:
Convert the real hydraulic press fixture into a simplified Mechanics of Materials model. Your sketch should show the cylindrical ram, flat plate, support blocks, applied load P, plate thickness t, ram diameter d, support opening s, total plate/support width b, and the potential punching shear sections AC and BD.

Student model placeholder: insert or draw the simplified model and load-transfer/stress-surface diagram here.
questions.instructor:
A correct idealization shows a vertical load P applied through the ram onto the plate, bearing stress distributed over the ram contact area, and two vertical punching shear sections AC and BD through the plate thickness at the loaded region.

For the student packet, provide a blank sketch space first. The instructor reference diagram can be shown after students attempt their own model if desired.

questions.title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State simplifying assumptions for average stress
Identify excluded effects
questions.student: State the assumptions used to convert the real press setup into the simplified Solid Mechanics model.
questions.instructor:
Assumptions may include static vertical load; ram is rigid relative to the plate; plate is checked using average stress; bearing stress is uniformly distributed over the idealized contact footprint; punching shear is uniformly distributed over sections AC and BD; support blocks are rigid; and stress concentrations, plate bending, plasticity, contact nonlinearity, and friction are neglected.

Expected answers do not need every assumption but should include the average-stress idealization.

questions.title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the average-stress calculation sequence
Select the correct areas before applying stress formulas
questions.student: Before calculating, describe the analysis sequence needed to determine punching shear stress and bearing stress.
questions.instructor:
The analysis sequence is: identify the load P; identify the contact/bearing area under the ram; identify the punching shear area along sections AC and BD; calculate τp = P/Ap for punching shear; calculate σb = P/Ab for bearing stress; compare the stress magnitudes; and state what material allowables would be needed for a design decision.

This helps students organize the calculation before substituting values.

questions.title: Boundary and Loading Conditions from Instructor Diagram
learningObjectives: Read load and support conditions from the idealized diagram
Focus on local stress instead of support reactions
questions.student: From the instructor diagram, identify the loading and support conditions used in the simplified model.
questions.instructor:
The cylindrical ram applies a downward compressive load P to the plate. The plate is supported below by two rigid support blocks on either side of the opening. The model focuses on local bearing under the ram and punching shear through sections AC and BD.

This replaces a full support-reaction analysis because the base learning goal is average stress, not beam bending.

questions.title: Potential Failure or Stress Surfaces
learningObjectives: Identify the surfaces over which stresses are evaluated
Distinguish contact area from shear-through-thickness area
questions.student: Identify the surfaces over which bearing stress and punching shear stress are evaluated.
questions.instructor:
Bearing stress is evaluated over the idealized contact footprint under the ram. Punching shear stress is evaluated through the plate thickness along sections AC and BD.

Students should distinguish a surface contact area from a shear-through-thickness area.

questions.title: Bearing Area Under the Ram
learningObjectives: Compute circular contact area
Use the stated bearing-area convention
questions.student: Determine the idealized contact area used to calculate average bearing stress under the cylindrical ram.
questions.instructor:
Using a circular contact footprint, Ab = πd2/4. With d = {{d}} {{d_unit}}, Ab = π({{d}} mm)2/4 = {{press_bearing_area_mm2}} mm2.

If an instructor wants a projected rectangular bearing area instead, that convention should be stated explicitly. This filled example uses the circular footprint area.

questions.title: Punching Shear Area Along Sections AC and BD
learningObjectives: Compute the two-section punching shear area
Use plate thickness in the shear area
questions.student: Determine the total idealized punching shear area through sections AC and BD.
questions.instructor:
Each punching shear section has idealized area dt. Since there are two sections, Ap = 2dt. With d = {{d}} {{d_unit}} and t = {{t}} {{t_unit}}, Ap = 2({{d}})({{t}}) = {{press_punching_area_mm2}} mm2.

This calculation uses the simplified two-section punching shear idealization shown in the instructor diagram.

questions.title: Average Punching Shear Stress
learningObjectives: Calculate average punching shear stress
Use N and mm units to obtain MPa
questions.student: Calculate the average punching shear stress developed in the plate along sections AC and BD.
questions.instructor:
Convert the load to N: P = {{press_load_N}} N. Then τp = P/Ap = {{press_load_N}}/{{press_punching_area_mm2}} = {{press_punching_shear_MPa}} MPa.

Use N and mm units so N/mm2 = MPa.

questions.title: Average Bearing Stress Under the Ram
learningObjectives: Calculate average bearing stress
Interpret bearing as compressive contact stress
questions.student: Calculate the average bearing stress developed on the plate surface under the cylindrical ram.
questions.instructor:
σb = P/Ab = {{press_load_N}}/{{press_bearing_area_mm2}} = {{press_bearing_stress_MPa}} MPa.

This is an average compressive contact stress, not a tensile stress.

questions.title: Compare Stress Magnitudes
learningObjectives: Compare average stress magnitudes
Avoid declaring failure without allowables
questions.student: Compare the calculated average punching shear stress and average bearing stress. Which stress quantity is larger?
questions.instructor:
Using the stated idealization, τp = {{press_punching_shear_MPa}} MPa and σb = {{press_bearing_stress_MPa}} MPa. The larger average stress quantity is {{press_larger_stress}} = {{press_larger_stress_MPa}} MPa.

Larger stress magnitude does not automatically mean governing failure unless shear and bearing allowables are known.

questions.title: Strength Factor of Safety and Mechanics-Based Modification
learningObjectives: Compute optional factors of safety
Recommend modifications based on stress-area relationships
questions.student: If allowable bearing and shear stresses are provided by the instructor, determine the factor of safety for bearing and punching shear. If the plate does not meet the required strength criterion, identify a mechanics-based modification that would reduce bearing stress or punching shear stress.
questions.instructor:
Using the optional allowables in the current input set, FOSshear = τallow/τp = {{tau_allow}}/{{press_punching_shear_MPa}} = {{press_fos_shear}}, and FOSbearing = σbearing,allow/σb = {{sigma_bearing_allow}}/{{press_bearing_stress_MPa}} = {{press_fos_bearing}}. The smaller simplified factor of safety is {{press_governing_fos}} for {{press_governing_fos_mode}}.

Possible modifications include increasing plate thickness t to reduce punching shear stress, increasing ram diameter d or using a load-spreading pad to reduce bearing stress, reducing load P, using a stronger plate material, or changing the support geometry to reduce local failure risk.

questions.title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Make a limited mechanics-based recommendation
State missing material data and excluded checks
questions.student: Use the mechanics results to make a limited engineering recommendation. Identify the larger calculated average stress and state what additional information is needed before accepting the fixture for service.
questions.instructor:
For the stated data and idealization, τp = {{press_punching_shear_MPa}} MPa and σb = {{press_bearing_stress_MPa}} MPa. The larger average stress is {{press_larger_stress}}.

However, accepting the fixture requires allowable shear stress, allowable bearing/compressive stress, required factor of safety, and possibly checks for plate bending, yielding, plastic indentation, contact nonlinearity, support deformation, and fixture alignment. The final recommendation should not overclaim safety without material allowables.

title: Shear and Bending-Moment Analysis of a Multi-Pulley Industrial Line Shaft
studentDocumentTitle: Student Homework Questions - Multi-Pulley Industrial Line Shaft
instructorDocumentTitle: Instructor Answers - Multi-Pulley Industrial Line Shaft
summary: An overhanging-beam problem integrating pulley load paths, bearing reactions, piecewise internal shear and moment, shear-force and bending-moment diagrams, and critical-station identification.
textbookChapters: Shear and moment diagrams for a beam
idealizedImageAlt: Instructor reference beam idealization of a line shaft supported by bearings A and B, with downward pulley forces F1 and F3, upward pulley force F2, and segment lengths L1 through L4.
problemStatement:
A production line uses a horizontal shaft to transmit motion among belt-driven conveyor and processing stations. Pillow-block bearings A and B support the shaft. The belt resultants are modeled as a downward force F1, an upward force F2, and a downward overhung force F3.

Model the bearings as vertical-force supports in the selected plane. Determine their reactions, construct the complete shear-force and bending-moment diagrams, and identify the shaft station carrying the largest absolute bending moment.
engineeringGoal: Use whole-shaft equilibrium and piecewise internal-resultant analysis to locate and quantify the absolute maximum bending moment before a later shaft stress or fatigue evaluation.

variables.label: Distance from pulley 2 to bearing B
Distance from B to overhung pulley 3

questions.title: System Function
learningObjectives: Describe the shaft's role in the production line.
questions.student: Identify the primary mechanical function of the line shaft and its pulleys in the production system.
questions.instructor: The shaft transmits rotation and torque among belt-driven stations. The pulleys introduce transverse belt resultants, while bearings A and B support the shaft and transfer those forces into the machine frame.

questions.title: External Pulley Loads
learningObjectives: Identify the transverse forces and their directions.
questions.student: List the three idealized pulley forces and state the direction of each force.
questions.instructor: F1 acts downward at pulley 1, F2 acts upward at pulley 2, and F3 acts downward at the overhung pulley 3.

questions.title: Bearing Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: State the reactions admitted by the bearing model.
questions.student: How are bearings A and B idealized in the selected loading plane, and which reactions do they provide?
questions.instructor: Each bearing is modeled as a simple support that supplies a vertical reaction but no reaction couple. Axial and out-of-plane reactions are outside this two-dimensional model.

questions.title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace transverse pulley loads to the supporting structure.
questions.student: Trace the load path from the belts and pulleys to the machine foundation.
questions.instructor: Belt tensions create resultant forces on the pulleys; the pulleys load the shaft; the shaft transfers transverse force through bearings A and B; and the bearing housings and machine frame carry the reactions to the foundation.

questions.title: Likely Critical Stations
learningObjectives: Anticipate where moment extrema can occur.
questions.student: Before calculating, identify the stations that must be checked for a maximum or minimum bending moment.
questions.instructor: Check the two bearings and all three pulley stations. With only concentrated forces, shear is constant between stations, so moment is linear and an extremum occurs where shear changes sign or at a boundary station.

questions.title: Relevant Internal Resultants
learningObjectives: Select the internal resultants required for the stated analysis.
questions.student: Which internal resultants are required to evaluate the shaft as a beam in the selected plane?
questions.instructor: The required resultants are transverse shear V and bending moment M. Torsion, axial force, and loading in the perpendicular plane require separate models if present.

questions.title: Governing Input Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify the inputs controlling reactions and diagrams.
questions.student: Identify the force and geometry parameters needed for the two-dimensional shear-and-moment analysis.
questions.instructor: The inputs are F1, F2, F3 and segment lengths L1 through L4, together with the stated force directions and bearing locations.

questions.title: Student-Generated Shaft Idealization
learningObjectives: Translate the physical shaft into a beam FBD.
questions.student: Before viewing the reference idealization, draw the complete shaft FBD. Show bearings A and B, reactions Ay and By, forces F1 through F3, lengths L1 through L4, and coordinate x measured rightward from A.
questions.instructor: A valid FBD shows A at x = 0; pulley 1 at L1; pulley 2 at L1 + L2; B at L1 + L2 + L3; and pulley 3 one L4 beyond B. The assumed bearing reactions are shown upward, with F1 and F3 downward and F2 upward.
questions.gradingNotes: Require all forces, stations, dimensions, and a coordinate direction before equations are written.

questions.title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions defining the model's scope.
questions.student: State the assumptions used to reduce the line shaft to a planar beam model.
questions.instructor: Assume static concentrated pulley resultants, a straight slender shaft, small deformation, ideal point supports, and forces acting in one plane. Neglect shaft and pulley self-weight unless included in the resultants, bearing width, stress concentrations, torsion, fatigue, dynamics, and loading in the perpendicular plane.

questions.title: Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan a complete reaction and internal-loading solution.
questions.student: List the calculation sequence for finding the reactions, shear diagram, moment diagram, and governing station.
questions.instructor: Define the sign convention and station coordinates; apply whole-shaft equilibrium for Ay and By; step through the concentrated forces to obtain piecewise shear; integrate shear or use moment equilibrium to obtain moment; enforce the free-end boundary condition; and compare the absolute moment at every candidate station.

questions.title: Station Coordinates
learningObjectives: Express every station using the assigned segment lengths.
questions.student: Using x measured from A, write the coordinates of pulley 1, pulley 2, bearing B, and pulley 3.
questions.instructor: Pulley 1: x = L1. Pulley 2: x = L1 + L2. Bearing B: x = L1 + L2 + L3. Pulley 3: x = L1 + L2 + L3 + L4.

questions.title: Equilibrium Equations
learningObjectives: Formulate independent whole-shaft equilibrium equations.
questions.student: Take upward force as positive. Write independent equilibrium equations for the two bearing reactions.
questions.instructor:
Vertical equilibrium gives Ay + By + F2 - F1 - F3 = 0.

Taking counterclockwise moment about A as positive gives By(L1 + L2 + L3) + F2(L1 + L2) - F1L1 - F3(L1 + L2 + L3 + L4) = 0.

questions.title: Bearing Reactions
learningObjectives: Calculate both bearing reactions with correct directions.
questions.student: Determine Ay and By. Report each magnitude and direction, and verify vertical-force equilibrium.
questions.instructor:
Ay = {{line_Ay_N}} N {{line_Ay_direction}} and By = {{line_By_N}} N {{line_By_direction}}.

The final running shear after all forces is {{line_force_check_N}} N; its zero value verifies vertical-force equilibrium apart from rounding.
questions.gradingNotes: Give full credit only when the overhung F3 moment arm includes L4.
questions.commonMistakes: A frequent error is placing F3 at bearing B or assigning the upward F2 the wrong sign.

questions.title: Shear-Force Diagram Ordinates
learningObjectives: Calculate the shear in every shaft segment.
questions.student: Construct the shear-force diagram. Report the constant shear in segments A-to-pulley 1, pulley 1-to-pulley 2, pulley 2-to-B, B-to-pulley 3, and immediately beyond pulley 3.
questions.instructor:
Using the stated sign convention, the segment shears are:

  • A to pulley 1: {{line_V1_N}} N
  • Pulley 1 to pulley 2: {{line_V2_N}} N
  • Pulley 2 to B: {{line_V3_N}} N
  • B to pulley 3: {{line_V4_N}} N
  • Beyond pulley 3: {{line_V5_N}} N

questions.title: Bending-Moment Diagram Ordinates
learningObjectives: Calculate moment at all load and support stations.
questions.student: Construct the bending-moment diagram by accumulating the signed area under the shear diagram. Report the moment at A, pulley 1, pulley 2, bearing B, and pulley 3.
questions.instructor:
The bending moments are:

  • A: {{line_MA_Nm}} N·m
  • Pulley 1: {{line_M1_Nm}} N·m
  • Pulley 2: {{line_M2_Nm}} N·m
  • Bearing B: {{line_MB_Nm}} N·m
  • Pulley 3/free end: {{line_M3_Nm}} N·m

The diagram is continuous and linear between concentrated-force stations.

questions.title: Piecewise Shear Function
learningObjectives: Express the shear force as a piecewise function.
questions.student: Write V(x) as a piecewise function for the four physical shaft segments, using x measured from A.
questions.instructor:
Let x1 = L1, x2 = L1 + L2, xB = L1 + L2 + L3, and x3 = xB + L4.

V = Ay for 0 < x < x1; V = Ay - F1 for x1 < x < x2; V = Ay - F1 + F2 for x2 < x < xB; and V = Ay - F1 + F2 + By for xB < x < x3.

questions.title: Piecewise Bending-Moment Function
learningObjectives: Express bending moment over the full shaft.
questions.student: Write a compact expression for M(x) over the shaft using bracket terms or provide an equivalent piecewise function.
questions.instructor:
With ⟨z⟩ = 0 for z < 0 and ⟨z⟩ = z otherwise,

M(x) = Ayx - F1⟨x - x1⟩ + F2⟨x - x2⟩ + By⟨x - xB⟩ - F3⟨x - x3⟩.

Use N and m, or divide N·mm results by 1000 to obtain N·m.

questions.title: Absolute Maximum Bending Moment
learningObjectives: Locate and quantify the governing bending moment.
questions.student: Determine the largest absolute bending moment, its signed value, and its location along the shaft.
questions.instructor: The largest absolute bending moment is {{line_Mmax_abs_Nm}} N·m. Its signed value is {{line_Mmax_signed_Nm}} N·m at the {{line_Mmax_station}}, located {{line_Mmax_x_mm}} mm from A.
questions.gradingNotes: Students must compare positive and negative ordinates by absolute value.

questions.title: Diagram and Overhang Interpretation
learningObjectives: Interpret sign changes and the influence of the overhung load.
questions.student: Explain why the moment becomes negative before bearing B and how the overhung pulley force affects the diagram.
questions.instructor: The shear becomes negative after pulley 1, so the moment decreases and crosses zero before reaching pulley 2. The overhung downward force F3 requires the B-to-pulley-3 segment to carry positive shear toward the free-end zero-moment condition; equivalently, it creates a negative moment of magnitude F3L4 at bearing B.

questions.title: Engineering Assessment and Model Limits
learningObjectives: Communicate the governing result and next design checks.
questions.student: Give a concise engineering assessment: identify the station to check first, suggest one way to reduce bending demand, and state at least two important limitations of this model.
questions.instructor: {{line_assessment}}
questions.commonMistakes: Do not treat this planar static bending result as a complete shaft design; torsion, fatigue, stress concentrations, and loading in the perpendicular plane may govern.
