title: Rear Suspension Linkage Pin Safety Check for a Mountain Bike
summary: A context-rich mechanics problem on rear suspension linkage forces, double-shear pin stress, and factor of safety.
idealizedImageAlt: Instructor idealized suspension linkage model with load, points, dimensions, and link angle.
problemStatement:
A mountain-bike or lightweight e-bike product team is reviewing the rear suspension linkage that supports rider load through a seat support member and shock absorber linkage. During riding, a vertical load from the rider is transmitted through the saddle into a curved support member, then into frame-mounted pins and the shock/link assembly.

As a junior mechanical engineer, you must simplify the real suspension assembly into a mechanics model and determine whether the pins at B and C have adequate resistance against shear failure under the specified design load. The analysis is limited to static equilibrium and average double-shear stress in the pins. Detailed dynamic loading, fatigue, bearing pressure, bushing wear, and frame deformation are outside the base problem.
engineeringGoal: Determine the forces transmitted through the suspension linkage and evaluate the factor of safety of pins B and C against shear failure. Identify the governing pin and make a limited mechanics-based recommendation for the specified static load case.

variables.label: Horizontal distance from A to B
Horizontal distance from B to C
Vertical offset between B and C
Shear failure stress of pin material
Number of shear planes per pin

questions.title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Identify the structural function of a linkage
Connect the real product to load transfer
questions.gradingNotes: Good answers should emphasize force transfer and support of load, not only comfort or product aesthetics.
questions.student: What is the primary structural function of the rear suspension linkage shown in the industry-context image?
questions.instructor: The linkage supports the rider load and transfers it from the saddle or seat support into the bicycle frame through the frame pivot at C and the shock/link connection at B-D.

questions.title: External Load
learningObjectives: Identify the applied load
Relate a physical rider load to an idealized point load
questions.student: Where is the external load applied in the idealized problem, and what physical action does it represent?
questions.instructor:
The external load P is applied downward at point A, representing the vertical load transmitted from the rider through the saddle to the suspension member.

Students should not distribute the load throughout the frame unless the instructor explicitly modifies the problem.

questions.title: Supports and Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Identify idealized supports
Recognize a two-force member
questions.student: Identify the support or connection locations that constrain the seat support member in the idealized model.
questions.instructor:
The seat support member is pinned to the frame at C and connected to the shock/link at B. The shock/link BD is treated as a two-force member, so the force at B acts along BD. Pin C provides reaction components on the seat support member.

This problem is not a fixed-beam problem. The key idealizations are pin support at C and two-force member BD at B.

questions.title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace the load path through a linkage
Name the pin-connected components that transfer load
questions.student: Using the component list, trace the load path from the rider load to the bicycle frame.
questions.instructor:
One acceptable load path is: rider load at saddle → curved seat support member → pin C and shock/link attachment at B → shock/link BD → lower frame joint at D → bicycle frame. The load is shared through the frame pin and the shock linkage.

The load path should explicitly mention the pins because they are the design-check components.

questions.title: Critical Components and Locations
learningObjectives: Identify the components included in a simplified stress check
Distinguish base-problem checks from detailed design checks
questions.student: Which components or locations are most critical for the simplified mechanics analysis?
questions.instructor: The critical components in the base problem are pins B and C because the design question asks for their factor of safety against shear failure. The seat support member and shock link also carry load, but their material and section properties are not provided for detailed stress checks.

questions.title: Critical Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Identify average shear stress as the target response
Explain double shear in connector design
questions.student: For pins B and C, identify the relevant mechanical response or failure mechanism considered in this problem.
questions.instructor:
The relevant response is average shear stress in each pin. Both pins are specified to be in double shear, so each pin has two resisting shear planes. The factor of safety is based on the material shear failure stress.

Bearing stress, bending of the pin, fatigue, bushing wear, and frame stresses are realistic concerns but are not part of the base MEEN 305 calculation.

questions.title: Relevant Geometric and Material Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify variables that control pin shear stress
Connect pin diameter to shear area and FOS
questions.student: Identify the geometric and material parameters that control the pin shear stress and factor of safety.
questions.instructor:
Relevant parameters are load P, horizontal distances from A to B and B to C, vertical offset between B and C, angle of shock/link BD, pin diameters dB and dC, number of shear planes ns, and shear failure stress τfail.

The pin area is A = πd2/4 and the total double-shear area is nsA. Students should connect pin diameter to shear area and factor of safety through τ = V/(nsA) and FOS = τfail/τ.

questions.title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Convert a product image into a 2D mechanics model
Draw a load-transfer diagram
questions.student:
Convert the real rear suspension assembly into a simplified 2D Mechanics of Materials model. Your sketch should show point A where load P is applied, pin locations B and C, lower joint D, shock/link BD, {{x_AB}} {{x_AB_unit}} and {{x_BC}} {{x_BC_unit}} horizontal dimensions, the {{y_BC}} {{y_BC_unit}} vertical offset, the {{theta_BD}} {{theta_BD_unit}} link angle, and the unknown pin/link forces.

Student model placeholder: insert or draw the simplified model and free-body/load-transfer diagram here.
questions.instructor:
A correct idealization treats the seat support as a rigid body acted on by the downward load P at A, the force from the two-force member BD at B, and reaction components at C. Pins B and C are later checked in double shear.

For the student packet, this should appear before the instructor reference model unless the activity is intentionally scaffolded.

questions.title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions for a simplified linkage model
Identify excluded real-design effects
questions.student: State the assumptions used to convert the real suspension assembly into the simplified Solid Mechanics model.
questions.instructor:
Appropriate assumptions include static loading; seat support treated as a rigid body for force analysis; BD treated as a two-force member; pins B and C treated as double-shear connectors; loads act in the plane of the idealized diagram; pin shear stress is averaged over the shear area; and fatigue, bearing stress, bushing wear, dynamic impact, shock nonlinearities, frame flexibility, and stress concentrations are neglected.

Expected answers do not need every assumption, but they should include rigid-body equilibrium, two-force member BD, and double-shear pin idealization.

questions.title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the solution sequence before substituting numbers
Connect equilibrium results to stress and FOS
questions.student: Before calculating, describe the analysis sequence needed to determine the factor of safety of pins B and C.
questions.instructor: The analysis sequence is: draw the FBD of the seat support member; use moment equilibrium about C to find the force in BD and the load at pin B; use force equilibrium to find the reaction at C; compute double-shear area for each pin; compute average shear stress τB and τC; compute FOSB and FOSC; identify the governing pin; and make a recommendation.

questions.title: Boundary and Loading Conditions from the Instructor Diagram
learningObjectives: Identify loads and idealized connections from a diagram
Avoid incorrect beam-support interpretations
questions.student: From the instructor diagram, identify the loading conditions and main connection idealizations.
questions.instructor:
The load P acts downward at A. Pin C connects the seat support to the frame and provides reaction components. Point B connects the seat support to the shock/link BD. Member BD is idealized as a two-force member, so the force at B acts along BD. Pins B and C are double-shear connectors for the stress check.

This replaces a standard beam-support interpretation. The critical idealizations are pin C and two-force member BD.

questions.title: Unknown Forces
learningObjectives: List unknown forces before solving equilibrium
Separate known force direction from unknown magnitude
questions.student: Identify the unknown forces that must be solved before calculating pin stresses.
questions.instructor:
The unknowns are the force in member BD at B and the reaction components at pin C. The force at B has a known direction along BD, but unknown magnitude. The reaction at C has unknown horizontal and vertical components.

Students should solve for forces before applying τ = V/A.

questions.title: Free-Body Diagram of the Seat Support Member
learningObjectives: Draw the FBD of a pin-connected body
Show two-force member force direction
questions.student: Draw the free-body diagram of the seat support member, showing P at A, the force from BD at B, and the reaction components at C.
questions.instructor:
A correct FBD shows P downward at A, force FBD at B acting along the shock/link direction, and reaction components Cx and Cy at pin C.

The direction of FBD on the upper member should be chosen consistently; if assumed opposite, a negative solution indicates the actual direction.

questions.title: Moment Equilibrium to Determine Link Force
learningObjectives: Use moment equilibrium about a pin
Include the vertical offset in a force moment arm
questions.commonMistakes: A common error is to omit the vertical offset yBC and use only xBC sinθBD as the moment arm.
questions.student: Use moment equilibrium about C to determine the magnitude of the force transmitted through shock/link BD.
questions.instructor:
The moment arm of P about C is xAB + xBC = {{bike_total_arm_mm}} mm. The force at B acts along BD. With xBC = {{x_BC}} {{x_BC_unit}}, yBC = {{y_BC}} {{y_BC_unit}}, and θBD = {{theta_BD}} {{theta_BD_unit}}, the resisting moment arm is xBC sinθBD + yBC cosθBD = {{bike_B_moment_arm_mm}} mm.

Therefore, FBD = P(xAB + xBC)/moment arm = {{bike_link_force_N}} N.

questions.title: Reaction Components at C
learningObjectives: Resolve an inclined link force
Use force equilibrium to find pin reaction components
questions.student: Using force equilibrium, determine the reaction components at pin C.
questions.instructor:
For the force direction that balances the applied load, the force at B on the seat support has components FBx = -FBD cosθBD = {{bike_B_force_x_N}} N and FBy = FBD sinθBD = {{bike_B_force_y_N}} N.

Force equilibrium gives Cx = {{bike_C_reaction_x_N}} N and Cy = {{bike_C_reaction_y_N}} N. The reaction magnitude is RC = {{bike_C_reaction_N}} N.

The magnitude of the reaction at C is used for the shear force in pin C.

questions.title: Shear Force Carried by Pin B
learningObjectives: Identify the shear force demand in a linkage pin
Connect link force to pin shear
questions.student: Determine the shear force carried by pin B.
questions.instructor:
Pin B transmits the force from the shock/link BD into the seat support. The shear force demand in pin B is taken as VB = FBD = {{bike_link_force_N}} N.

Because the problem states that pin B is in double shear, this total load is resisted over two shear planes.

questions.title: Shear Force Carried by Pin C
learningObjectives: Use reaction magnitude as pin shear demand
Avoid using only one reaction component for pin shear
questions.student: Determine the shear force carried by pin C.
questions.instructor:
Pin C transmits the reaction between the seat support and frame. The shear force demand in pin C is the reaction magnitude VC = RC = {{bike_C_reaction_N}} N.

Use the resultant reaction, not only one component, for the pin shear demand.

questions.title: Double-Shear Areas of Pins B and C
learningObjectives: Compute circular pin area
Apply double-shear resisting area
questions.student: Calculate the total double-shear resisting area for pins B and C.
questions.instructor:
For a circular pin, A = πd2/4. For pin B, AB = {{bike_pin_B_area_mm2}} mm2 and the total shear area is nsAB = {{bike_pin_B_double_area_mm2}} mm2. For pin C, AC = {{bike_pin_C_area_mm2}} mm2 and the total shear area is nsAC = {{bike_pin_C_double_area_mm2}} mm2.

Use N and mm units so that stress is in N/mm2 = MPa.

questions.title: Average Shear Stress in Pins B and C
learningObjectives: Compute average double-shear stress
Compare load and diameter effects
questions.student: Determine the average shear stress in pins B and C.
questions.instructor:
Pin B: τB = VB/(nsAB) = {{bike_link_force_N}}/{{bike_pin_B_double_area_mm2}} = {{bike_pin_B_shear_MPa}} MPa.

Pin C: τC = VC/(nsAC) = {{bike_C_reaction_N}}/{{bike_pin_C_double_area_mm2}} = {{bike_pin_C_shear_MPa}} MPa.

Pin C may have a smaller load than pin B but also has a smaller diameter, so it can still be more critical.

questions.title: Factor of Safety of Pins B and C
learningObjectives: Compute factor of safety against shear failure
Identify the governing pin
questions.student: Using τfail = {{tau_fail}} {{tau_fail_unit}}, determine the factor of safety of pins B and C against shear failure.
questions.instructor:
FOSB = τfail/τB = {{tau_fail}}/{{bike_pin_B_shear_MPa}} = {{bike_pin_B_fos}}.

FOSC = τfail/τC = {{tau_fail}}/{{bike_pin_C_shear_MPa}} = {{bike_pin_C_fos}}.

Pin {{bike_governing_pin}} has the lower factor of safety and is governing for the simplified shear check.

questions.title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Make a limited mechanics-based recommendation
State limitations of a simplified static pin check
questions.student: Use the mechanics results to make a limited engineering recommendation for the suspension pins. Also list additional failure modes or serviceability concerns that would need to be checked before approving the full suspension design.
questions.instructor:
For the simplified static shear check, pin B has τB = {{bike_pin_B_shear_MPa}} MPa and FOSB = {{bike_pin_B_fos}}. Pin C has τC = {{bike_pin_C_shear_MPa}} MPa and FOSC = {{bike_pin_C_fos}}. Pin {{bike_governing_pin}} is governing because it has the lower factor of safety. The simplified pin-shear recommendation is: {{bike_recommendation}}.

Final design acceptance requires a target design FOS and additional checks such as bearing stress at the pin holes, tear-out or net-section failure of the brackets, fatigue under repeated riding loads, shock absorber limits, bushing wear, pin bending, frame weld stresses, dynamic impact loading, and stiffness/deflection of the seat support.

title: Torque Distribution and Hollow-Shaft Sizing for a Multi-Gear Drive Shaft
summary: A multi-station torsion problem integrating torque equilibrium, internal torque diagrams, solid-shaft stress, governing-segment identification, and hollow-shaft sizing.
idealizedImageAlt: Instructor reference idealization of a multi-gear circular shaft with bearings at A and E, applied gear torques at B, C, D, and F, and labeled shaft segments.
problemStatement:
A manufacturing line uses a common rotating shaft to distribute mechanical power among several gear-driven stations. Each gear introduces or removes torque, so the internal torque changes from segment to segment.

The design team is evaluating the existing solid shaft and a tubular replacement with the same outer diameter. The base model includes shaft-axis torque only; gear forces, bending, fatigue, local stress concentrations, and dynamic effects are excluded.
engineeringGoal: Determine the signed internal torque and maximum torsional shear stress in every shaft segment, identify the governing segment, and select the minimum available tubular wall thickness that satisfies the allowable shear-stress requirement.

questions.title: Primary Function of the Shaft Assembly
learningObjectives: Identify the shaft assembly's role in the production system.
questions.student: State the primary structural and mechanical function of the shaft assembly.
questions.instructor: The shaft distributes torque and mechanical power among multiple gear-driven stations while the bearings support and align the rotating shaft.

questions.title: Applied Torsional Loads
learningObjectives: Identify the external actions included in the torsion model.
questions.student: Identify the external mechanical loads relevant to the base torsion analysis.
questions.instructor: The relevant loads are the applied torques TB, TC, TD, and TF at the four gear locations. Gear weights and transverse gear forces are excluded from the base torsion model.
questions.gradingNotes: Students should distinguish torque from force and power.

questions.title: Bearing Roles and Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Distinguish radial support from torsional restraint.
questions.student: Describe the mechanical role of bearings A and E in the simplified model.
questions.instructor: The bearings restrain transverse motion and support the shaft while permitting rotation. Ideal frictionless bearings do not supply reaction torque about the shaft axis.

questions.title: Torque Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace torque transfer through a multi-station shaft.
questions.student: Trace how torque is transmitted through the shaft from one gear station to another.
questions.instructor: Each gear adds or removes torque. The internal torque in any segment equals the algebraic sum of the external torques on one side of a cut through that segment.

questions.title: Predicting the Governing Segment
learningObjectives: Predict how the governing segment will be identified.
questions.student: Before calculating, explain how the governing solid-shaft segment will be identified.
questions.instructor: Because every solid-shaft segment has the same diameter, the segment with the largest absolute internal torque has the largest maximum torsional shear stress and governs.

questions.title: Parameters Controlling the Design
learningObjectives: Identify the inputs controlling shaft stress and wall thickness.
questions.student: Identify the parameters that control solid-shaft shear stress and tubular wall thickness. Explain whether the segment lengths affect the base stress calculation.
questions.instructor: Applied torques, shaft outer diameter, inner diameter or wall thickness, polar moment of inertia, and allowable shear stress control the design. Segment lengths describe the geometry and support optional angle-of-twist work, but they do not affect shear stress under Saint-Venant torsion.

questions.title: Student-Generated Shaft Idealization
learningObjectives: Create a multi-torque shaft model before viewing the reference figure.
questions.student: Before using the reference figure, draw a simplified shaft model showing points A through F, gear torques and directions, bearing locations, shaft segments, and shaft diameter. Establish a positive torque sign convention.
questions.instructor: A correct model idealizes the assembly as a circular shaft with concentrated torques at B, C, D, and F and ideal rotation-permitting bearings at A and E. Torque arrows and the positive sign convention must be unambiguous.
questions.gradingNotes: Students should attempt the model before seeing the instructor idealization.

questions.title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the torsion model.
questions.student: State the assumptions used in the base torsion model.
questions.instructor: Assume a circular prismatic shaft, homogeneous linearly elastic material, concentrated static torques, ideal bearings that do not resist shaft-axis torque, small deformation, and Saint-Venant torsion. Neglect transverse gear forces, bending, warping restraint, and local stress concentrations.

questions.title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan a complete segment-stress and sizing analysis.
questions.student: Outline the calculation sequence before substituting numbers.
questions.instructor: Choose a torque sign convention; verify overall torque equilibrium; cut each shaft segment and determine internal torque; construct the torque diagram; calculate solid-shaft shear stress; identify the governing torque; size the tubular shaft; round wall thickness upward to the available increment; and verify the selected thickness.

questions.title: Torque Sign Convention and Overall Equilibrium
learningObjectives: Verify shaft-axis torque equilibrium.
questions.student: Select a positive torque direction and verify overall torque equilibrium for the assigned gear torques.
questions.instructor: Using the signs supplied with the assignment, ΣT = TB + TC + TD + TF = {{gear_torque_sum_kNm}} kN·m. {{gear_equilibrium_assessment}}

questions.title: Internal Torque in Each Segment
learningObjectives: Calculate internal torque throughout a multi-load shaft.
questions.student: Determine the signed internal torque in segments AB, BC, CD, DE, and EF. Also report each magnitude.
questions.instructor:
Using cuts and the assigned sign convention: TAB = {{gear_T_AB_kNm}} kN·m, TBC = {{gear_T_BC_kNm}} kN·m, TCD = {{gear_T_CD_kNm}} kN·m, TDE = {{gear_T_DE_kNm}} kN·m, and TEF = {{gear_T_EF_kNm}} kN·m.

The corresponding magnitudes are {{gear_abs_T_AB_kNm}}, {{gear_abs_T_BC_kNm}}, {{gear_abs_T_CD_kNm}}, {{gear_abs_T_DE_kNm}}, and {{gear_abs_T_EF_kNm}} kN·m.
questions.commonMistakes: Do not replace the cumulative algebraic sum with the nearest applied gear torque.

questions.title: Internal Torque Diagram
learningObjectives: Construct and interpret an internal torque diagram.
questions.student: Construct the internal torque diagram along A-F and label the torque jump at every gear.
questions.instructor: The diagram is {{gear_T_AB_kNm}} kN·m on AB, then changes to {{gear_T_BC_kNm}} on BC, {{gear_T_CD_kNm}} on CD, {{gear_T_DE_kNm}} on DE, and {{gear_T_EF_kNm}} kN·m on EF. Each jump equals the signed applied torque at that gear. Bearing E creates no jump.

questions.title: Maximum Shear Stress in the Solid Shaft
learningObjectives: Calculate maximum torsional shear stress in every segment.
questions.student: For the assigned solid-shaft diameter, calculate the maximum torsional shear stress in every segment using τmax = 16|T|/(πd3).
questions.instructor: The segment stresses are τAB = {{gear_tau_AB_MPa}} MPa, τBC = {{gear_tau_BC_MPa}} MPa, τCD = {{gear_tau_CD_MPa}} MPa, τDE = {{gear_tau_DE_MPa}} MPa, and τEF = {{gear_tau_EF_MPa}} MPa.
questions.commonMistakes: Convert kN·m to N·mm before using millimeter section dimensions.

questions.title: Governing Shaft Segment
learningObjectives: Identify the segment controlling the tubular-shaft design.
questions.student: Identify the governing segment or segments and explain why they control the tubular-shaft design.
questions.instructor: {{gear_governing_segments}} {{gear_governing_verb}} with an internal torque magnitude of {{gear_governing_torque_kNm}} kN·m. The governing location carries the largest absolute internal torque, and the solid-shaft diameter is uniform.

questions.title: Tubular-Shaft Sizing Equation
learningObjectives: Derive the allowable-stress equation for a hollow circular shaft.
questions.student: Starting from τ = Tc/J, derive the equation for the maximum permissible tubular-shaft inner diameter.
questions.instructor:
For J = π(Do4 - Di4)/32 and c = Do/2,

τallow = 16TmaxDo/[π(Do4 - Di4)],

so Di,max = [Do4 - 16TmaxDo/(πτallow)]1/4 = {{gear_D_i_max_mm}} mm.

questions.title: Minimum Tubular Wall Thickness
learningObjectives: Select a manufacturable wall thickness from a theoretical minimum.
questions.student: Determine the theoretical minimum tubular wall thickness and select the smallest thickness available in the assigned increment. Explain the rounding direction.
questions.instructor: tmin = (Do - Di,max)/2 = {{gear_t_min_mm}} mm. Round upward to the assigned increment, giving {{gear_t_selected_mm}} mm. The corresponding selected inner diameter is {{gear_D_i_selected_mm}} mm.

questions.title: Selected-Thickness Verification
learningObjectives: Verify a practical wall-thickness selection.
questions.student: Recalculate the maximum shear stress using the selected wall thickness and determine the allowable-stress utilization.
questions.instructor: The selected wall gives τmax = {{gear_tau_selected_MPa}} MPa and utilization τmax/τallow = {{gear_utilization}}. {{gear_thickness_assessment}}

questions.title: Bearing E and Equal Adjacent Torques
learningObjectives: Explain why an ideal bearing does not change internal torque.
questions.student: Explain why bearing E does not create a jump in the torque diagram and why segments DE and EF carry the same torque.
questions.instructor: An ideal bearing does not apply torque about the shaft axis. Internal torque is therefore unchanged across E, so DE and EF carry the same signed internal torque until the external torque at F is applied.

questions.title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Make a bounded shaft recommendation.
questions.student: Provide a concise recommendation for the tubular shaft and identify important limitations of the base model.
questions.instructor:
{{gear_recommendation}}

Detailed design must additionally evaluate bending from gear forces, combined stress, fatigue, keyways and shoulders, stress concentrations, angular twist, critical speed, bearing loads, manufacturing tolerances, and applicable standards.
questions.gradingNotes: Students should not claim full machine safety from the pure-torsion calculation alone.

title: Optimal Support Placement for Transporting a Precast Concrete Column
summary: A symmetric overhanging-beam problem integrating load paths, support reactions, piecewise shear and moment functions, diagram construction, and minimax support-placement optimization.
idealizedImageAlt: Instructor reference idealization of a uniformly loaded precast column on two truck supports with equal end overhangs.
problemStatement:
A precast-concrete manufacturer must transport a long, uniform column from the casting yard to a construction site. Two timber or elastomeric support blocks carry the member on a flatbed trailer. The column self-weight acts continuously over its length, and poor support placement can create excessive transport-induced bending.

Model the column as a prismatic beam of total length L under uniform load w, with two simple supports placed at equal offsets a from the ends.
engineeringGoal: Determine the equal support offset that minimizes the absolute maximum bending moment, construct the corresponding shear-force and bending-moment diagrams, and identify the governing positive and negative moment locations.

questions.title: Role of the Transport Supports
learningObjectives: State the structural role of the transport supports.
questions.student: State the role of the two transport supports.
questions.instructor: The supports transfer the column self-weight to the trailer while controlling bending demand in the transported member.

questions.title: Dominant External Loading
learningObjectives: Identify the dominant load in the simplified model.
questions.student: Identify the dominant external load acting on the column in the simplified transport model.
questions.instructor: The column self-weight is represented by a uniform distributed load w over the full length L.

questions.title: Support Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Describe the support idealizations and admitted reactions.
questions.student: How should the two transport supports be idealized, and which reactions do they provide?
questions.instructor: Model them as simple point supports that permit rotation and provide upward vertical reactions but no reaction moments.

questions.title: Load Path to the Road
learningObjectives: Trace the column load to the road surface.
questions.student: Trace the load path from the column to the road.
questions.instructor: Column self-weight transfers through the transport blocks to the trailer bed and frame, then through the suspension and axles to the road surface.

questions.title: Expected Critical Moment Locations
learningObjectives: Anticipate the locations of positive and negative moment extrema.
questions.student: Before calculating, where should the governing positive and negative bending moments be expected?
questions.instructor: Negative moments occur at the two supports because of the overhangs. By symmetry, the maximum positive moment occurs at the beam center.

questions.title: Symmetric Support Arrangement
learningObjectives: Justify equal offsets using geometry and loading symmetry.
questions.student: Why is it reasonable to place the supports at equal offsets from the two ends?
questions.instructor: The uniform column geometry and distributed loading are symmetric, so the optimal idealized static support arrangement is also symmetric.

questions.title: Support-Placement Tradeoff
learningObjectives: Explain the competing effects controlled by support location.
questions.student: Explain why placing the supports either too close to the ends or too close to the center is unfavorable.
questions.instructor: Supports near the ends leave a long interior span and produce a large positive center moment. Supports near the center create long overhangs and large negative support moments.

questions.title: Student-Generated Beam Idealization
learningObjectives: Translate the transport system into a beam model and FBD.
questions.student: Before viewing the reference figure, draw a beam of total length L carrying uniform load w. Place supports at x = a and x = L - a, and label the equal overhangs and reactions.
questions.instructor: A valid FBD shows a uniformly loaded beam from x = 0 to x = L, upward reactions R1 and R2 at the two supports, and equal end overhangs a.
questions.gradingNotes: Students should create their model before seeing the instructor reference idealization.

questions.title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions defining the model's scope.
questions.student: State the assumptions used to represent the transport condition.
questions.instructor: Assume a straight, uniform, prismatic column; uniformly distributed self-weight; static loading; point supports; continuous contact with both supports; and small deformation. Neglect road dynamics, tie-down forces, local bearing stress, and cracking.

questions.title: Optimization Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the mechanics and optimization sequence.
questions.student: List the calculation sequence needed to find the optimal support offset.
questions.instructor: Use symmetry and equilibrium to find the reactions; derive piecewise shear and moment functions; identify the negative support and positive center moments; equate their magnitudes; solve for a/L; and construct the optimized diagrams.

questions.title: Support Locations and Reactions
learningObjectives: Identify support coordinates and reaction directions.
questions.student: Identify the support locations and reaction directions using coordinate x measured from the left end.
questions.instructor: The supports are at x = a and x = L - a. Each provides an upward vertical reaction.

questions.title: Support Reactions
learningObjectives: Determine reactions using symmetry and equilibrium.
questions.student: Use symmetry and vertical equilibrium to determine R1 and R2.
questions.instructor: The total distributed load is wL. Therefore R1 = R2 = wL/2 = {{column_reaction_kip}} kip. The total column weight is {{column_total_weight_kip}} kip.

questions.title: Piecewise Beam Regions
learningObjectives: Partition the beam for internal-resultant equations.
questions.student: Divide the column into the three regions required for piecewise shear and moment analysis.
questions.instructor: Region I: 0 ≤ x < a; Region II: a ≤ x ≤ L - a; Region III: L - a < x ≤ L.

questions.title: Piecewise Shear Functions
learningObjectives: Derive shear force in all beam regions.
questions.student: Using upward force as positive, derive V(x) in each region.
questions.instructor: Region I: V = -wx. Region II: V = wL/2 - wx. Region III: V = wL - wx.

questions.title: Piecewise Bending-Moment Functions
learningObjectives: Derive bending moment in all beam regions.
questions.student: Derive M(x) in each region using M(0) = 0.
questions.instructor:
Region I: M = -wx2/2.

Region II: M = -wx2/2 + (wL/2)(x - a).

Region III: M = -wx2/2 + (wL/2)(x - a) + (wL/2)[x - (L - a)].

questions.title: Negative Support Moment
learningObjectives: Calculate the negative moment at either support.
questions.student: Determine the bending moment at either support.
questions.instructor: Ms = -wa2/2. At the optimal offset, Ms = {{column_support_moment_kipft}} kip·ft.

questions.title: Positive Center Moment
learningObjectives: Calculate the positive moment at beam center.
questions.student: Determine the positive bending moment at x = L/2.
questions.instructor: Mc = wL2/8 - wLa/2. At the optimal offset, Mc = {{column_center_moment_kipft}} kip·ft.

questions.title: Minimax Condition
learningObjectives: Formulate the minimax support-placement condition.
questions.student: Apply a minimax argument by making the governing positive and negative moment magnitudes equal.
questions.instructor: Set |Ms| = Mc: wa2/2 = wL2/8 - wLa/2. Canceling w gives a2 + La - L2/4 = 0.

questions.title: Optimal Support Offset
learningObjectives: Solve for the optimal dimensionless support offset.
questions.student: Solve the minimax equation and report a as a fraction of L and as a numerical value for the assigned column.
questions.instructor: The physically admissible root is a = [(√2 - 1)/2]L = {{column_optimal_ratio}}L. For L = {{column_L}} {{column_L_unit}}, a = {{column_optimal_offset_ft}} ft. The support spacing is {{column_support_spacing_ft}} ft.

questions.title: Minimized Maximum Moment
learningObjectives: Calculate the minimized absolute maximum bending moment.
questions.student: Determine the minimized absolute maximum bending moment.
questions.instructor: |M|max = [ (3 - 2√2)/8 ]wL2 = {{column_moment_coefficient}}wL2 = {{column_max_abs_moment_kipft}} kip·ft.

questions.title: Optimized Shear and Moment Diagrams
learningObjectives: Construct and label optimized internal-resultant diagrams.
questions.student: Draw the optimized shear-force and bending-moment diagrams. Label the values at both ends, immediately before and after each support, and at the center.
questions.instructor:
Shear values from left to right are: end {{column_V_left_kip}} kip; left support minus {{column_V_left_support_minus_kip}} kip; left support plus {{column_V_left_support_plus_kip}} kip; center {{column_V_center_kip}} kip; right support minus {{column_V_right_support_minus_kip}} kip; right support plus {{column_V_right_support_plus_kip}} kip; right end {{column_V_right_kip}} kip.

The moment diagram is quadratic and continuous: zero at both free ends, {{column_support_moment_kipft}} kip·ft at each support, and {{column_center_moment_kipft}} kip·ft at center.

questions.title: Engineering Recommendation and Limits
learningObjectives: Communicate a support-placement recommendation with appropriate limits.
questions.student: Give a concise support-placement recommendation and state at least one important limitation of the model.
questions.instructor: {{column_recommendation}}
questions.gradingNotes: A complete recommendation should include the offset from each end and at least one omitted real-system effect.
questions.commonMistakes: Do not recommend the center-to-center support spacing as though it were the end offset.

title: Load Sharing in a Three-Spoke Mobility Wheel Under Axle Load
summary: A context-rich mechanics problem on load sharing in a rigid-rim wheel with three equal axial spokes.
idealizedImageAlt: Instructor idealization of the three-spoke wheel with hub, spokes, load, radius, and 120 degree spacing.
problemStatement:
A product engineering team is evaluating a lightweight three-spoke wheel used in a mobility device, small robotic platform, or compact ground-support vehicle. A vertical axle load is transferred from the hub into the spoke network and then into the rigid outer rim and ground contact region.

Because the rim is much stiffer than the spokes, the first-order mechanics model treats the rim as rigid. The spokes are modeled as axial members made from the same material and having the same cross-sectional area. The engineering task is to determine how the axle load is shared among the three spokes and to identify which spoke force has the largest magnitude before a later stress or safety-factor check is performed.
engineeringGoal: Determine the axial force in each of the three spokes under the applied axle load. Use the result to identify which spoke is in tension, which spokes are in compression, and what additional information would be required to perform a complete stress or factor-of-safety check.

variables.label: Vertical axle load applied at hub A

questions.title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Identify the structural function of the wheel-spoke system
Use load-transfer language
questions.student: What is the primary structural function of the wheel-spoke system?
questions.instructor:
The system transfers the vertical axle load from the hub through the spokes into the rigid rim and then into the ground. The spokes serve as axial load-carrying members that connect the hub to the rim.

Good answers should use load-transfer language rather than only naming parts of the wheel.

questions.title: External Load
learningObjectives: Identify where the external load enters the system
Distinguish hub load from rim/ground contact
questions.student: Where is the external load applied, and what is its direction?
questions.instructor:
The external load P is applied at the hub/axle point A and acts vertically downward. In the numerical case, P = {{P}} {{P_unit}}.

Students should not apply the load at the rim or ground contact. The axle load enters the wheel at the hub.

questions.title: Supports and Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Describe the rigid-rim boundary assumption
Explain why spoke attachment points are fixed relative to the rim
questions.student: Identify the effective support or constraint in the idealized model.
questions.instructor:
The rim is idealized as rigid and supported through ground contact. The points where the spokes attach to the rim are treated as fixed relative to the rigid rim. The hub can displace slightly under load, causing axial deformation of the spokes.

This is not a simple pin-support reaction problem. The key modeling assumption is the rigid rim plus deformable axial spokes.

questions.title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace load from axle to ground
Include the rim in the load path
questions.student: Trace the load path from the axle to the ground.
questions.instructor:
The load path is: axle load at hub A → axial forces in spokes AB, AC, and AD → rigid outer rim → ground contact region → ground/supporting surface.

The rim should be included explicitly because it transfers the spoke loads to the ground.

questions.title: Critical Components
learningObjectives: Identify the components included in the simplified analysis
Separate base-model checks from later design checks
questions.student: Which components are critical for the simplified analysis?
questions.instructor:
The three spokes are the critical components for the simplified analysis because they carry the axial forces created by the vertical axle load. The rim is assumed rigid and is not stress-checked in this base problem.

If the problem is extended later, rim bending, hub connection details, and spoke stress can be checked.

questions.title: Critical Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Identify axial force as the target response
Interpret tension and compression in the spokes
questions.student: For each critical component, identify the relevant mechanical response.
questions.instructor:
The relevant mechanical response is axial force in each spoke. The vertical spoke AB develops tensile force, while the two lower inclined spokes AC and AD develop compressive force in the idealized rigid-rim model. A full stress analysis would require each spoke cross-sectional area.

This is an important conceptual point: equal material and area do not imply equal force in all spokes because force distribution depends on compatibility and geometry.

questions.title: Relevant Geometric and Material Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify the variables controlling load sharing
Explain why equal stiffness causes E and area to cancel in the base force solution
questions.student: Identify the geometric and material parameters that control the spoke forces.
questions.instructor:
Relevant parameters are the applied axle load P, spoke radius/length r, spoke angular spacing θ, cross-sectional area As, and elastic modulus E. Since all spokes have the same material, cross-sectional area, and length, their axial stiffnesses are equal, so the force distribution depends mainly on geometry and compatibility.

In the base problem, the actual force values are independent of E and As because the stiffnesses are equal; however, E and As would be needed to compute displacements or stresses.

questions.title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Convert a real wheel into a 2D mechanics model
Represent rigid rim and axial spokes
questions.student:
Convert the real wheel into a simplified 2D Mechanics of Materials model. The model should show the rigid rim, hub point A, three spokes AB, AC, and AD, the downward axle load P at A, the spoke radius r, and the {{theta}} {{theta_unit}} angular spacing.

Student model placeholder: insert or draw the simplified model and free-body/compatibility diagram here.
questions.instructor:
A correct student idealization shows a rigid circular rim with three axial spokes connected to a central hub. The external load P acts downward at the hub. The spokes are treated as axial members of equal stiffness because they have the same material, cross-sectional area, and length.

This should be completed before the final mechanics equations are developed.

questions.title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions for an axial-spoke model
Recognize when tension-only spokes would invalidate the compression result
questions.student: State the assumptions used to convert the real wheel into the simplified mechanics model.
questions.instructor:
Assumptions may include static loading; rim is rigid; spokes are straight axial members; spokes have the same material, cross-sectional area, and length; deformations are small; the hub displacement is vertical by symmetry; bending of the rim and spokes is neglected; local hub/rim connection stresses are neglected; and the lower spokes can carry compression in the idealized model.

The last assumption is important. If the physical spokes were tension-only wires, the lower spokes would not carry compression and the model would need to be modified.

questions.title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan a compatibility and equilibrium solution
Explain why equilibrium alone is insufficient
questions.student: Before calculating, describe the sequence needed to determine the force in each spoke.
questions.instructor:
Use symmetry to recognize that the two lower spoke forces are equal. Use deformation compatibility to relate the axial deformation of each spoke to the vertical displacement of the hub. Use equal axial stiffness to relate deformation to spoke force. Finally, apply vertical force equilibrium at the hub to solve for the spoke forces.

The correct solution requires compatibility plus equilibrium, not equilibrium alone.

questions.title: Boundary and Loading Conditions from Instructor Diagram
learningObjectives: Read loading and idealization from the diagram
Distinguish axial load sharing from rim bending
questions.student: From the instructor diagram, identify the loading condition and the primary idealization of the rim and spokes.
questions.instructor:
The hub A is subjected to a downward load P. The rim is treated as rigid, so the spoke attachment points B, C, and D remain fixed relative to the rim. The spokes are treated as equal-stiffness axial members.

This problem is about load sharing through compatible axial deformation, not about bending stress in the rim.

questions.title: Unknown Spoke Forces
learningObjectives: Identify unknown internal spoke forces
Use symmetry to reduce unknowns
questions.student: Identify the unknown internal forces that must be determined.
questions.instructor:
The unknowns are the axial forces FB, FC, and FD in spokes AB, AC, and AD. By symmetry, FC = FD.

Use a sign convention. In this solution, positive axial force means tension; negative axial force means compression.

questions.title: Symmetry of Hub Displacement
learningObjectives: Use symmetry to infer displacement direction
Reduce the compatibility model to one displacement variable
questions.student: Explain why the hub displacement can be assumed vertical in the idealized model.
questions.instructor:
The geometry and loading are symmetric about the vertical centerline. The two lower spokes are mirror images, and the external load has no horizontal component. Therefore the horizontal displacement of the hub is zero and the hub displacement is vertical.

This lets students use one displacement variable, such as δ, for the vertical hub displacement.

questions.title: Compatibility of Spoke Deformations
learningObjectives: Relate hub displacement to axial deformation
Interpret elongation and shortening signs
questions.student: Let the hub move downward by a small displacement δ. Determine the axial deformation of each spoke in terms of δ.
questions.instructor:
The vertical spoke AB elongates by δ. Each lower spoke has a vertical projection equal to cos(60°) = 1/2 relative to the hub displacement direction, so each lower spoke shortens by δ/2. Therefore, ΔB = δ and ΔC = ΔD = -δ/2.

The negative sign for the lower spokes means shortening, which corresponds to compression under the chosen tension-positive sign convention.

questions.title: Force-Deformation Relations
learningObjectives: Use equal axial stiffness to relate force and deformation
Derive force ratios before using equilibrium
questions.student: Using equal axial stiffness ks = EAs/r for all spokes, express FB, FC, and FD in terms of ks and δ.
questions.instructor:
FB = ksδ. FC = FD = -ksδ/2. Therefore, FC = FD = -FB/2.

This is the compatibility step that makes the problem determinate.

questions.title: Equilibrium and Spoke Force Values
learningObjectives: Apply vertical force equilibrium at the hub
Compute spoke forces and interpret signs
questions.student: Write vertical force equilibrium at the hub A using the spoke force components and the downward load P. Then determine the axial force in each spoke for P = {{P}} {{P_unit}}.
questions.instructor:
Using positive tension along each spoke, vertical equilibrium is FB - (1/2)FC - (1/2)FD - P = 0. Substituting FC = FD = -FB/2 gives (3/2)FB = P.

Therefore, FB = 2P/3 = {{wheel_force_B_kN}} kN, and FC = FD = -P/3 = {{wheel_force_C_kN}} kN. Thus spoke AB is in {{wheel_force_B_abs_kN}} kN tension, and spokes AC and AD are each in {{wheel_force_C_abs_kN}} kN compression.

Report both sign and physical meaning. A negative result should not be discarded; it indicates compression relative to the tension-positive convention.

questions.title: Governing Spoke Force Magnitude
learningObjectives: Compare axial force magnitudes
Identify which member would be checked first
questions.student: Which spoke has the largest axial force magnitude?
questions.instructor:
The vertical spoke AB has the largest magnitude, |FB| = {{wheel_force_B_abs_kN}} kN. The lower spokes each have magnitude |FC| = |FD| = {{wheel_force_C_abs_kN}} kN.

The governing spoke for force magnitude is {{wheel_governing_spoke}} with {{wheel_governing_force_kN}} kN. This identifies which member would be checked first if area and material strength were provided.

questions.title: Stress, Stiffness, and Engineering Recommendation
learningObjectives: State data needed for stress or FOS
Make a limited engineering recommendation
Recognize tension-only limitations
questions.student: What additional information would be needed to compute stress or factor of safety in the spokes? Use the mechanics results to make a limited engineering recommendation for the wheel-spoke system.
questions.instructor:
To compute stress, the cross-sectional area As of each spoke is needed, using σi = Fi/As. To compute factor of safety, allowable tensile and compressive stresses or material strengths are needed. If the spokes are tension-only, compression capacity is not valid and the physical model must be reconsidered.

For the current optional area value, the stress estimates are σB = {{wheel_stress_B_MPa}} MPa, σC = {{wheel_stress_C_MPa}} MPa, and σD = {{wheel_stress_D_MPa}} MPa, with negative stress indicating compression. If E and As are used for a stiffness extension, δ = 2Pr/(3EAs) = {{wheel_hub_displacement_mm}} mm.

For the idealized model, the vertical spoke AB carries the largest axial force, {{wheel_force_B_abs_kN}} kN in tension. The two lower spokes each carry {{wheel_force_C_abs_kN}} kN in compression. A detailed design decision requires spoke cross-sectional area, material tensile/compressive allowable stresses, and confirmation that the lower spokes are capable of carrying compression. If the spokes are tension-only, this rigid-rim equal-spoke model is not physically acceptable without modification.

title: Spring-Loaded Coupling Rod Assembly Under Tensile Load
summary: A context-rich mechanics problem on spring compression, axial member elongation, load sharing, and deformation compatibility.
idealizedImageAlt: Instructor reference idealization of the spring-loaded coupling rod assembly with rigid plates, compression spring, side bolts, dimensions, and tensile load.
problemStatement:
A mechanical design team is evaluating a spring-loaded coupling assembly used in an industrial machine fixture. The assembly uses a central coupling rod, three rigid plates, two side bolts, and a compression spring to transmit a tensile load while allowing a controlled change in spacing.

When the coupling rod is pulled, the spring compresses, the side bolts elongate, and the active central-rod segment elongates. The measured distance between lower plate C and upper eye E therefore changes through several deformation mechanisms and must be predicted using a compatible assembly model.
engineeringGoal: Determine the final distance d between points C and E after the tensile load is applied, accounting for compression of the spring, elongation of the side bolts, and elongation of the active coupling-rod segment.

variables.label: Initial distance between C and E
Diameter of each side bolt and active rod
Active coupling-rod length from B to E
Active side-bolt length between A and C

questions.title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Identify the structural purpose of a compliant coupling assembly.
questions.student: What is the primary structural function of the spring-loaded coupling assembly?
questions.instructor: The assembly transfers tensile load while allowing controlled displacement through spring compression and elastic deformation of the steel members. It provides a compliant load path rather than a fully rigid connection.
questions.gradingNotes: Good answers should connect load transfer and controlled compliance to the mechanics of the assembly.

questions.title: External Loads
learningObjectives: Identify the external force pair producing tension in the central rod.
questions.student: Where are the external loads applied, and what are their directions?
questions.instructor: Equal and opposite tensile loads P are applied at upper eye E and the lower end of the coupling rod. The loading pair places the central rod in tension.

questions.title: Constraints and Idealized Connections
learningObjectives: Identify the assembly constraints needed for a compatibility model.
questions.student: Identify the effective constraints and connections in the system.
questions.instructor: Plates A, B, and C are treated as rigid. The spring connects A and B and compresses under load. Identical side bolts connect A and C and elongate in tension. The central rod transfers load through the assembly and elongates over its active length.
questions.gradingNotes: This is an assembly-compatibility problem rather than a conventional fixed-support reaction problem.

questions.title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace load through all deformable and rigid components.
questions.student: Using the component list, trace the load path through the coupling rod, plates, bolts, and spring.
questions.instructor: A suitable path is applied tensile load → central coupling rod → rigid plate or collar contact → compression spring and rigid plates → side bolts → lower plate C and the opposite load application. The spring compresses while the bolts and rod elongate.
questions.commonMistakes: The load path must include both the compression spring and the tension-loaded side bolts.

questions.title: Components Controlling the Final Distance
learningObjectives: Distinguish deformable components from rigid transfer components.
questions.student: Which components are most important for determining the final distance d?
questions.instructor: The compression spring, active central-rod segment, and side bolts control d. The rigid plates establish the load path and compatibility relationships, but their deformation is neglected.

questions.title: Relevant Mechanical Responses
learningObjectives: Select the relevant response for each component and reject unsupported checks.
questions.student: For each critical component, identify the mechanical response considered in this problem.
questions.instructor: The spring undergoes compression. The side bolts and central coupling rod undergo axial elongation. Plates are assumed rigid. Failure, fatigue, local contact, and buckling are outside the base problem because the necessary strength and detail data are not supplied.

questions.title: Relevant Geometry and Material Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify the inputs controlling spring and axial-member deformation.
questions.student: Identify the loading, geometric, and material parameters needed to determine the final distance d.
questions.instructor: The required inputs are P, d0, k, db, Es, nb, LE, and Lb. Bolt/rod area is Ab = πdb2/4. The rigid-plate and equal-load-sharing assumptions are also required.

questions.title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Convert the real assembly into a rigid-plate, spring, and axial-member model.
questions.student: Before using the reference figure, draw a simplified Mechanics of Materials model. Show rigid plates A, B, and C; coupling rod and eye E; side bolts; spring; applied tensile load P; and distance d. Include force and deformation directions.
questions.instructor: A correct model treats A, B, and C as rigid plates; the spring as a linear compression spring; the side bolts as identical axial tension members; and the coupling rod as an axial tension member. Distance d is formed from compatible plate and rod motions.
questions.gradingNotes: Provide students with drawing space before revealing the instructor reference idealization.

questions.title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the simplified compatibility analysis.
questions.student: State the assumptions used to convert the physical assembly into the simplified mechanics model.
questions.instructor: Typical assumptions are rigid plates A, B, and C; a linear spring of stiffness k; identical side bolts sharing load equally; linear-elastic steel; small deformation; concentric loading; and neglected nut, thread, contact, bending, shear, and friction effects.

questions.title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan a multi-contribution displacement calculation.
questions.student: Before calculating, describe the sequence of analysis needed to determine final distance d.
questions.instructor: Determine spring, rod, and bolt forces; compute spring compression; compute active-rod elongation; compute side-bolt elongation; establish how each changes C-to-E spacing; sum the compatible contributions; and add the increase to initial distance d0.

questions.title: Loading Conditions from the Instructor Diagram
learningObjectives: Interpret the instructor reference model and its response quantity.
questions.student: From the instructor reference diagram, identify the loading condition and principal mechanical idealizations.
questions.instructor: The assembly is subjected to equal and opposite tensile loads P. Plates A, B, and C are rigid; the spring is linear; side bolts and central rod deform axially; and response is evaluated by tracking the change in distance between C and E.

questions.title: Internal Forces and Load Sharing
learningObjectives: Determine component forces using equilibrium, symmetry, and identical-member behavior.
questions.student: For P = {{P}} {{P_unit}} and nb = {{n_b}} identical side bolts, determine the force in the spring, active coupling-rod segment, and each side bolt.
questions.instructor: The spring carries {{spring_force_kip}} kip in compression. The active coupling rod carries {{spring_rod_force_kip}} kip in tension. Symmetry and identical bolt stiffness give {{spring_bolt_force_kip}} kip in tension in each of the {{n_b}} side bolts.
questions.commonMistakes: Divide the total bolt load by the number of identical bolts; do not assign the full load to every bolt.

questions.title: Spring Compression
learningObjectives: Apply the linear spring force-displacement relationship.
questions.student: Calculate the spring compression using k = {{k}} {{k_unit}}.
questions.instructor: δs = P/k = {{P}}/{{k}} = {{spring_compression_in}} in. This compression increases the C-to-E distance for the modeled geometry.

questions.title: Coupling-Rod Elongation
learningObjectives: Calculate axial elongation of the active coupling-rod segment.
questions.student: Calculate the elongation of the active coupling-rod segment. First determine member area from db = {{d_b}} {{d_b_unit}}.
questions.instructor:
Ab = π({{d_b}} in)2/4 = {{spring_member_area_in2}} in2. Then

δrod = PLE/(AbEs) = {{spring_rod_elongation_in}} in.
questions.commonMistakes: With load in kip and area in in2, use Es in ksi = kip/in2.

questions.title: Side-Bolt Elongation
learningObjectives: Calculate elongation of parallel, equally loaded axial members.
questions.student: Calculate the elongation of each side bolt. Clearly use the force carried by one bolt rather than the total applied load.
questions.instructor:
Each bolt carries P/nb = {{spring_bolt_force_kip}} kip. Therefore

δbolt = (P/nb)Lb/(AbEs) = {{spring_bolt_elongation_in}} in.

All identical bolts have the same elongation and act in parallel; their elongations are not added to one another.
questions.commonMistakes: The load divides among parallel bolts, but their common plate-to-plate elongation does not divide or sum.

questions.title: Final Distance Between C and E
learningObjectives: Combine compatible deformation contributions into an assembly dimension.
questions.student: Determine the final distance d between C and E after loading. Show why each deformation contribution increases or decreases the measured distance.
questions.instructor:
Spring compression increases E-to-A spacing, rod elongation increases E-to-B spacing, and side-bolt elongation increases A-to-C spacing. Thus

Δd = δs + δrod + δbolt = {{spring_compression_in}} + {{spring_rod_elongation_in}} + {{spring_bolt_elongation_in}} = {{spring_distance_increase_in}} in.

d = d0 + Δd = {{d0}} + {{spring_distance_increase_in}} = {{spring_final_distance_in}} in.
questions.gradingNotes: Require a compatibility argument, not only arithmetic addition of three values.

questions.title: Stiffness-Based Interpretation
learningObjectives: Relate the largest deformation contribution to component stiffness.
questions.student: Which deformation contribution dominates the change in distance d, and why?
questions.instructor: The dominant contribution is {{spring_dominant_component}}, with magnitude {{spring_dominant_value_in}} in. For the baseline values, spring compression is much larger than either steel-member elongation because the spring is intentionally much more compliant.

questions.title: Stiffness-Based Modification
learningObjectives: Propose a mechanics-based change that reduces final displacement.
questions.student: If final distance d must be reduced, identify and justify a mechanics-based design modification.
questions.instructor: Possible changes include increasing spring stiffness k, increasing bolt/rod diameter, reducing active member lengths, reducing applied load, or changing assembly geometry. For the baseline case, increasing k is usually the most effective single change because spring compression dominates.

questions.title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Make a limited recommendation without exceeding the model's evidence.
questions.student: Use the mechanics results to make a limited engineering recommendation about the assembly response. State what additional information would be required before service approval.
questions.instructor: For P = {{P}} kip, the predicted final distance is {{spring_final_distance_in}} in, and {{spring_dominant_component}} governs displacement. This model is suitable for preliminary displacement prediction. Service approval additionally requires allowable stresses, fatigue requirements, spring travel and solid-height checks, local contact and thread details, plate stiffness, tolerances, and manufacturing or inspection information.
questions.gradingNotes: The recommendation should answer the displacement question without claiming that strength or durability has been verified.

title: Thermal Expansion Force in a Steam Pipe Between Turbine Housings
summary: A thermal-deformation problem integrating hollow-pipe geometry, support flexibility, compatibility, axial force, stress, and engineering assessment.
idealizedImageAlt: Instructor reference idealization of a hollow steam pipe connected between two turbine attachment points represented by equal axial springs.
problemStatement:
A power-plant engineering team is reviewing a short steel steam pipe connecting two turbine housings. The pipe is assembled at installation temperature T1 and later reaches operating temperature T2. If free, the pipe would change length by αLΔT.

The turbine attachment points provide finite axial restraint. They are modeled as identical linear springs, so the pipe's thermal deformation is shared between elastic deformation of the pipe and movement of both turbine attachments.
engineeringGoal: Determine the thermally induced axial force exerted on each turbine housing and the corresponding axial stress in the pipe. Compare the stress with yield and make a limited recommendation about attachment flexibility and further design checks.

variables.label: Axial stiffness of each turbine attachment

questions.title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Connect the pipe's process function to its structural load-transfer role.
questions.student: What are the primary process and structural functions of the pipe-turbine assembly?
questions.instructor: The pipe transfers steam between turbine housings while maintaining a sealed connection. Structurally, it transfers thermally induced axial loads into the turbine attachments when free thermal deformation is restrained.
questions.gradingNotes: Good answers should mention both fluid transport and mechanical load transfer.

questions.title: Source of Mechanical Loading
learningObjectives: Distinguish thermal loading from a directly applied force.
questions.student: What creates the mechanical loading in this problem? Is an independent external axial force applied to the pipe?
questions.instructor: The temperature change causes the pipe to seek a free length change αLΔT. Finite restraint at the turbine attachments opposes that change and creates axial force. No independent external axial load is applied in the base model.

questions.title: Supports and Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Interpret finite attachment stiffness as partial axial restraint.
questions.student: Identify the support idealization used for turbine attachments A and B.
questions.instructor: Each turbine attachment is modeled as an axial linear spring of stiffness k. The pipe ends are therefore partially restrained and can move as the attachments deform under the thermally induced force.
questions.commonMistakes: The attachment points are not perfectly fixed in this model.

questions.title: Thermal Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace thermally induced force from the pipe into the foundation.
questions.student: Trace the load path created when thermal deformation of the pipe is restrained.
questions.instructor: The pipe attempts to change length; the turbine attachments resist that motion; axial force develops in the pipe; equal and opposite forces pass through the flanged connections into the turbine housings, machine supports, and foundation.

questions.title: Critical Components
learningObjectives: Identify components controlling the one-dimensional response.
questions.student: Which components are most important for this simplified Mechanics of Materials analysis?
questions.instructor: The hollow steel pipe is critical because it develops axial stress, and the two turbine attachments are critical because their stiffness controls the degree of restraint. Detailed flange, bolt, gasket, casing, and foundation stresses are not evaluated.

questions.title: Relevant Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Select force and stress responses supported by the provided data.
questions.student: What mechanical responses should be evaluated in the base problem?
questions.instructor: Evaluate thermally induced axial force and average axial pipe stress. Comparing stress with yield provides a limited strength interpretation. Pressure stress, creep, fatigue, local flange response, bending, and stability require additional models and data.

questions.title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Connect each input to thermal deformation, axial compliance, or strength.
questions.student: Identify the geometric, thermal, material, and support parameters that control the pipe force and stress.
questions.instructor: The required inputs are pipe length L, outer diameter Do, wall thickness t, temperatures T1 and T2, attachment stiffness k, elastic modulus E, thermal-expansion coefficient α, and yield stress σy. Inner diameter and area follow from the pipe geometry.

questions.title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Convert the plant assembly into a one-dimensional thermal compatibility model.
questions.student: Before using the reference figure, develop a simplified mechanics model showing the hollow pipe, turbine attachment points, axial support stiffness, pipe length, temperature change, and unknown thermally induced axial force.
questions.instructor: A correct idealization shows a uniform hollow pipe of length L connected between two axial springs, each of stiffness k. The pipe has free thermal deformation αLΔT, but attachment restraint creates axial force.
questions.gradingNotes: Students should attempt the model before the instructor reference idealization is revealed.

questions.title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the thermal compatibility solution.
questions.student: State the assumptions used to convert the real pipe-turbine assembly into the simplified model.
questions.instructor: Typical assumptions are uniform pipe temperature; a uniform hollow cross section; one-dimensional axial behavior; linear-elastic pipe material and supports; identical attachment stiffness at A and B; small deformation; rigid flange load transfer; and neglected pressure, bending, thermal gradients, creep, fatigue, routing flexibility, and local connection effects.

questions.title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the calculation from geometry through engineering interpretation.
questions.student: Before calculating, describe the sequence needed to determine the force exerted on the turbine housings.
questions.instructor: Compute inner diameter and pipe area; determine ΔT and free thermal deformation; write compatibility among free deformation, pipe elastic deformation, and both support displacements; solve for axial force; compute average pipe stress; compare with yield; then state a limited recommendation.

questions.title: Boundary Conditions from the Reference Diagram
learningObjectives: Interpret the pipe-and-springs reference model.
questions.student: From the instructor reference diagram, identify the pipe boundary conditions and support idealizations.
questions.instructor: Pipe AB is connected at each end to a turbine attachment modeled as an axial spring of stiffness k. Both attachment points can move under force, so the pipe is partially rather than fully restrained.

questions.title: Unknown Thermally Induced Force
learningObjectives: Define the unknown interaction force and its action on each component.
questions.student: Identify the unknown axial force produced by restrained thermal deformation and describe its action on the pipe and turbine housings.
questions.instructor: The unknown is the thermally induced axial pipe force. For the assigned temperatures, the pipe is in {{thermal_force_state}} and exerts equal-magnitude, opposite-direction forces on the two turbine attachments.

questions.title: Hollow-Pipe Cross-Sectional Area
learningObjectives: Calculate the material area of a hollow circular section.
questions.student: For Do = {{D_o}} {{D_o_unit}} and t = {{t}} {{t_unit}}, determine the inner diameter and cross-sectional area of the steel pipe.
questions.instructor:
Di = Do - 2t = {{thermal_inner_diameter_in}} in.

A = π[Do2 - Di2]/4 = {{thermal_pipe_area_in2}} in2.
questions.commonMistakes: Use the annular material area, not the area of a solid bar with diameter Do.

questions.title: Free Thermal Deformation
learningObjectives: Calculate signed free thermal deformation.
questions.student: Calculate the temperature change and the pipe deformation that would occur if the pipe were unrestrained.
questions.instructor:
ΔT = T2 - T1 = {{T_2}} - {{T_1}} = {{thermal_delta_T_F}}°F. The pipe experiences {{thermal_action}}.

δT = αLΔT = {{thermal_free_expansion_in}} in, with magnitude {{thermal_free_expansion_magnitude_in}} in.
questions.gradingNotes: A positive value denotes free expansion; a negative value denotes free contraction.

questions.title: Compatibility Equation
learningObjectives: Formulate compatibility for a member between two flexible supports.
questions.student: Write the signed compatibility equation relating free thermal deformation, elastic deformation of the pipe, and movement of both turbine attachments.
questions.instructor:
Using a compression-positive sign convention for F,

αLΔT = FL/(AE) + 2F/k.

The pipe compliance is {{thermal_pipe_compliance_in_per_kip}} in/kip, the combined support compliance is {{thermal_support_compliance_in_per_kip}} in/kip, and total compliance is {{thermal_total_compliance_in_per_kip}} in/kip. The factor 2 accounts for movement at both turbine attachments.
questions.commonMistakes: Do not omit one attachment displacement or treat the two end springs as a single spring of stiffness k.

questions.title: Thermally Induced Pipe Force
learningObjectives: Solve compatibility for the pipe-support interaction force.
questions.student: Solve for the thermally induced axial force in the pipe and the force magnitude exerted on each turbine housing.
questions.instructor:
F = δT/[L/(AE) + 2/k] = {{thermal_pipe_force_kip}} kip using compression-positive thermal-force convention. Thus the pipe carries {{thermal_pipe_force_magnitude_kip}} kip in {{thermal_force_state}} and exerts that force magnitude on each turbine attachment.

The pipe elastic contribution has magnitude {{thermal_pipe_elastic_deformation_in}} in. Each support moves {{thermal_support_displacement_each_in}} in, for a combined support movement of {{thermal_support_displacement_total_in}} in.

questions.title: Pipe Stress and Yield Comparison
learningObjectives: Calculate average axial stress and make a limited yield comparison.
questions.student: Determine the average axial stress in the pipe and compare its magnitude with σy = {{sigma_y}} {{sigma_y_unit}}.
questions.instructor: σ = F/A = {{thermal_pipe_stress_ksi}} ksi; its magnitude is {{thermal_pipe_stress_magnitude_ksi}} ksi in {{thermal_stress_state}}. The yield-to-stress ratio is {{thermal_yield_ratio}}. {{thermal_yield_assessment}}
questions.gradingNotes: This is an average axial-stress comparison, not a pressure-piping code assessment or a full factor of safety evaluation.

questions.title: Stiffness Interpretation
learningObjectives: Predict how support stiffness changes thermal force.
questions.student: Explain how attachment stiffness k affects the thermal force. Which compliance contribution dominates for the assigned values?
questions.instructor: Larger k permits less attachment movement, restrains more thermal deformation, and increases pipe force toward the fully restrained limit. Smaller k reduces force by allowing more movement. For the assigned values, {{thermal_dominant_compliance}} is the larger compliance contribution.

questions.title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Make a mechanics-based recommendation without overclaiming safety.
questions.student: Use the force and stress results to make a limited engineering recommendation. Identify additional checks required before accepting the installation.
questions.instructor: The pipe develops {{thermal_pipe_force_magnitude_kip}} kip in {{thermal_force_state}} and an average stress magnitude of {{thermal_pipe_stress_magnitude_ksi}} ksi. {{thermal_yield_assessment}} The turbine allowable nozzle loads should be compared with the computed attachment force. If more flexibility is needed, consider pipe-routing flexibility, engineered expansion provisions, or less rigid attachments. Final acceptance also requires pressure, flange, bolt, gasket, weld, creep, fatigue, thermal-gradient, stability, and code checks.
questions.gradingNotes: The response should not claim full design safety from the average axial-stress calculation alone.
