title: Suspended Industrial Equipment Pod Supported by Two Inclined Steel Cables
summary: A context-rich mechanics problem on 2D cable equilibrium, axial cable stress, minimum diameter, and factor of safety.
idealizedImageAlt: Instructor reference idealization of the two-cable suspended equipment system.
problemStatement:
An industrial facility is installing a compact sensor or inspection equipment pod in a maintenance bay. The pod is suspended above the floor using two steel wire cables connected to wall-mounted brackets on opposite structural columns. The cable angles are not symmetric, so the load is not shared equally between the two cables.

As a junior facilities or mechanical engineer, evaluate whether the cable support arrangement can safely carry the equipment weight. The goal is not to redesign the full support structure, but to use Mechanics of Materials tools to determine cable tensions, cable tensile stresses, and the required cable diameters or factors of safety.
engineeringGoal: Determine whether the two inclined steel cables can safely support the suspended equipment pod under the specified static loading. Identify the cable with the larger tensile demand and determine either the minimum required cable diameter for a specified factor of safety or the actual factor of safety for selected cable diameters.

questions.title: Primary Function of the Suspended Support System
learningObjectives: Connect the real suspended system to its structural load-transfer function.
questions.student: What is the primary structural function of the suspended equipment support system?
questions.instructor: The system supports a suspended equipment pod and transfers its weight through two inclined steel cables into wall-mounted anchor brackets and then into the building structure.
questions.gradingNotes: Good answers should mention support of the pod, weight transfer, cables, wall anchors, and building structure.

questions.title: External Load and Weight
learningObjectives: Identify the payload weight and where it acts in the idealized model.
questions.student: Where is the external load applied, and what physical quantity creates it?
questions.instructor: The external load is the equipment weight applied downward at the lower ring or connector B. The load is W = mg. For m = {{m}} {{m_unit}} and g = {{g}} {{g_unit}}, W = {{cable_weight_N}} N.
questions.commonMistakes: Students sometimes place the pod weight at A or C. It acts at the payload/lower connector B.

questions.title: Supports and Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Identify support idealizations for a cable-supported particle-equilibrium model.
questions.student: Identify the supports or boundary constraints in the real system.
questions.instructor: The wall-mounted brackets at A and C support the cables. In the idealized model, A and C are fixed anchor locations that provide cable reaction forces along the cable directions. The lower point B is a ring or shackle connection where the two cable forces and the payload weight meet.
questions.gradingNotes: The most important free-body diagram is the lower joint B, not the entire wall frame.

questions.title: Load Path to the Building Structure
learningObjectives: Trace the load path from payload to support structure.
questions.student: Using the component list, trace the load path from the equipment pod to the building structure.
questions.instructor: Equipment pod weight → lower ring/shackle at B → tension in cable AB and cable BC → wall anchors A and C → structural columns or walls → building frame/foundation.

questions.title: Critical Components
learningObjectives: Identify which members are checked in the base mechanics problem.
questions.student: Using the load path, identify the components most likely to be critical for this problem.
questions.instructor: The critical components are the two steel cables AB and BC because they carry the payload through axial tension. The lower ring and wall anchor brackets are also part of the load path, but connector dimensions are not provided for a detailed connector stress check in the base problem.

questions.title: Critical Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Choose the relevant mechanics response and reject irrelevant checks for the base model.
questions.student: For each critical component, identify the relevant mechanical response or failure mechanism and rank them by importance.
questions.instructor: The most important response is axial tensile stress in the cables. Secondary connector shear or bearing could be checked only if shackle, pin, bolt, or bracket dimensions are supplied. Buckling is not relevant because cables are tension-only members, and cable bending is neglected in this base model.

questions.title: Relevant Geometry and Material Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify the variables controlling cable tension, stress, and FOS.
questions.student: Identify the geometric and material parameters that control the cable stress and factor of safety.
questions.instructor: Relevant parameters include cable angles θAB = {{theta_AB}} {{theta_AB_unit}} and θBC = {{theta_BC}} {{theta_BC_unit}}, mass m, gravitational acceleration g, cable diameters dAB and dBC, cable cross-sectional areas AAB and ABC, cable failure stress σfail, and required factor of safety.

questions.title: Student-Generated Cable Idealization
learningObjectives: Convert the real suspended system into a 2D particle-equilibrium model.
questions.student: Convert the real system into a simplified 2D Mechanics of Materials model. The model should show support points A and C, lower joint B, cable members AB and BC, cable angles, the downward load W = mg, and the unknown cable tensions.
questions.instructor: A correct idealization is a 2D particle-equilibrium model of joint B with two cable tensions directed away from B along cables BA and BC and a downward weight W. The cables are idealized as two-force tension members.
questions.gradingNotes: This should be completed before students rely on the instructor reference diagram, unless the activity is intentionally scaffolded.

questions.title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions needed for the simplified equilibrium and stress model.
questions.student: State the assumptions used to convert the real support system into the simplified mechanics model.
questions.instructor: The equipment pod is modeled as a point load at B; cable self-weight is neglected; each cable is straight and massless; each cable is a two-force tension member; loading is static; anchor locations are fixed; material behavior is represented only by failure stress; and connector flexibility, bracket stresses, fatigue, and installation tolerances are neglected.

questions.title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the solution sequence from equilibrium to design recommendation.
questions.student: Before calculating, describe the sequence of analysis required to evaluate the cables.
questions.instructor: Draw the FBD of joint B; write equilibrium in x and y; solve for TAB and TBC; compute cable area from selected diameter or required area from allowable stress; compute σ = T/A; compute FOS = σfail/σ; and make an engineering recommendation.

questions.title: Boundary Conditions from the Instructor Diagram
learningObjectives: Interpret the support and cable-force idealizations from the instructor diagram.
questions.student: From the instructor reference diagram, identify the boundary conditions and support idealizations.
questions.instructor: Points A and C are fixed wall anchor locations. The cables are attached to these supports and carry only tensile force along their own axes. Joint B is treated as a pin/ring where the two cable tensions and the downward weight act concurrently.
questions.commonMistakes: This is not a beam support problem; do not introduce moment reactions at B.

questions.title: Unknown Cable Forces
learningObjectives: Identify the two unknown member forces before writing equilibrium equations.
questions.student: Identify the unknown forces that must be solved before the cable stresses can be evaluated.
questions.instructor: The unknowns are the two cable tensions TAB and TBC. These are the force magnitudes transmitted by cables AB and BC. At joint B, each tension acts along its cable direction away from B.

questions.title: Equilibrium Equations at Joint B
learningObjectives: Write 2D equilibrium equations for an asymmetric cable joint.
questions.student: Draw the free-body diagram of joint B and write the x- and y-equilibrium equations.
questions.instructor:
Using +x to the right and +y upward:

ΣFx = -TAB cos({{theta_AB}}°) + TBC cos({{theta_BC}}°) = 0.

ΣFy = TAB sin({{theta_AB}}°) + TBC sin({{theta_BC}}°) - W = 0.
questions.commonMistakes: A common error is switching sine and cosine because the angles are measured from the horizontal.

questions.title: Cable Tensions
learningObjectives: Solve the two equilibrium equations for cable tensions.
questions.student: Using m = {{m}} kg and g = {{g}} m/s2, solve for TAB and TBC.
questions.instructor: W = mg = {{cable_weight_N}} N. From horizontal equilibrium, TAB cos({{theta_AB}}°) = TBC cos({{theta_BC}}°). Solving with vertical equilibrium gives TAB = {{cable_T_AB_N}} N and TBC = {{cable_T_BC_N}} N. The larger cable tension is in {{cable_governing_tension_member}}.
questions.gradingNotes: For the default geometry, cable AB carries the larger tension because the angles are asymmetric.

questions.title: Minimum Cable Diameter for Required FOS
learningObjectives: Determine required cable area and diameter from tension and allowable stress.
questions.student: If the cable material has failure normal stress σfail = {{sigma_fail}} MPa and the required factor of safety is {{FOS_req}}, determine the minimum required diameter of each cable.
questions.instructor: The allowable stress is σallow = σfail/FOSreq = {{sigma_fail}}/{{FOS_req}} = {{cable_allowable_stress_MPa}} MPa. Required area is Areq = T/σallow. Therefore AAB,req = {{cable_A_AB_req_mm2}} mm2, dAB,min = {{cable_d_AB_min_mm}} mm; ABC,req = {{cable_A_BC_req_mm2}} mm2, dBC,min = {{cable_d_BC_min_mm}} mm.
questions.gradingNotes: Because MPa = N/mm2, using T in N gives area in mm2 and diameter in mm.

questions.title: Strength FOS Check for Selected Diameters
learningObjectives: Compute cable stress and FOS for selected cable diameters.
questions.student: Now suppose cable AB has diameter dAB = {{d_AB}} mm and cable BC has diameter dBC = {{d_BC}} mm. Determine the normal stress and factor of safety in each cable.
questions.instructor: AAB = π({{d_AB}})2/4 = {{cable_A_AB_mm2}} mm2, so σAB = TAB/AAB = {{cable_sigma_AB_MPa}} MPa and FOSAB = {{sigma_fail}}/{{cable_sigma_AB_MPa}} = {{cable_FOS_AB}}. ABC = π({{d_BC}})2/4 = {{cable_A_BC_mm2}} mm2, so σBC = TBC/ABC = {{cable_sigma_BC_MPa}} MPa and FOSBC = {{sigma_fail}}/{{cable_sigma_BC_MPa}} = {{cable_FOS_BC}}. The governing selected-diameter FOS is {{cable_governing_fos}} in {{cable_governing_fos_member}}.

questions.title: Strength-Based Modification
learningObjectives: Propose mechanics-based changes when a factor of safety requirement is not met.
questions.student: If either cable does not meet the required factor of safety, identify a mechanics-based modification that would increase the factor of safety.
questions.instructor: Possible modifications include increasing the diameter of the governing cable, selecting a cable material with larger failure stress, reducing the supported mass, or changing the cable geometry to reduce the tension in the governing cable. For this numerical case, {{cable_design_recommendation}}.

questions.title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Make a limited engineering recommendation based on cable strength and missing connector checks.
questions.student: Using the mechanics results, make a limited engineering recommendation for the suspended equipment support. Include connector or anchor checks that would be needed before final service approval.
questions.instructor: The governing load case is the static weight of the {{m}} kg equipment pod, W = {{cable_weight_N}} N. Cable {{cable_governing_tension_member}} carries the larger tension. For the minimum-diameter design, use dAB ≥ {{cable_d_AB_min_mm}} mm and dBC ≥ {{cable_d_BC_min_mm}} mm before rounding up to standard cable sizes. For dAB = {{d_AB}} mm and dBC = {{d_BC}} mm, the selected-diameter check gives FOSAB = {{cable_FOS_AB}} and FOSBC = {{cable_FOS_BC}}; therefore, {{cable_design_recommendation}}. Final service acceptance still requires separate verification of wall anchors, brackets, shackles, pins, fatigue if cyclic loading exists, and installation quality.
questions.gradingNotes: The recommendation should return to the real support system without claiming connector or anchor safety from cable stress alone.

title: Suspended Industrial Equipment Platform Supported by Stainless-Steel Wires
summary: A two-level suspended-platform problem integrating rigid-body equilibrium, axial wire deformation, displacement compatibility, and small-angle rotation.
idealizedImageAlt: Instructor reference idealization of two rigid suspended members connected to each other and the ceiling by four vertical tension wires.
problemStatement:
A manufacturing facility is installing a suspended service platform that supports a compact equipment module above the production floor. The assembly has an upper rigid member and a lower rigid member connected by stainless-steel tension wires. The upper member is suspended from fixed overhead anchors by a second pair of wires.

Because load P is applied eccentrically to the lower member, the four wires do not carry equal forces. Their unequal elastic elongations cause both rigid members to translate and rotate.
engineeringGoal: Determine the downward displacement of the equipment load and the small-angle tilt of each rigid member. Identify the wire carrying the largest force and the deformation contribution that most strongly influences platform motion.

variables.label: Length of each upper wire ED and FC
Length of each lower wire AH and BC
Length of upper rigid member DC
Length of lower rigid member AB
Distance from D to lower-wire point H
Distance from A to the payload

questions.title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Identify the structural purpose of the suspended platform system.
questions.student: What is the primary structural function of the suspended platform system?
questions.instructor: The system supports an equipment load and transfers it through lower rigid member AB, lower wires AH and BC, upper rigid member DC, upper wires ED and FC, and finally into the fixed overhead support.
questions.gradingNotes: Students should describe support and force transfer, not merely identify the assembly as a platform.

questions.title: External Load and Eccentricity
learningObjectives: Explain why payload position affects support-wire forces.
questions.student: Where is the external load applied, and why does its position matter?
questions.instructor: Load P is applied to lower rigid member AB at an eccentric location. Its position controls the moment about the lower-wire attachment points, causing unequal wire forces and unequal elongations that rotate the member.

questions.title: Supports and Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Distinguish fixed anchors from movable rigid members.
questions.student: Identify the supports and boundary constraints in the system.
questions.instructor: The upper ends of wires ED and FC are attached to fixed overhead anchors E and F. Members AB and DC are rigid but are free to translate and rotate as the four tension wires elongate.
questions.commonMistakes: Do not model either horizontal member as a fixed beam.

questions.title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace load through both levels of the suspended assembly.
questions.student: Trace the load path from the equipment load to the building structure.
questions.instructor: Equipment load P → lower rigid member AB → lower wires AH and BC → upper rigid member DC → upper wires ED and FC → fixed overhead support → building structure.

questions.title: Critical Components
learningObjectives: Separate deformable wires from rigid load-distribution members.
questions.student: Which components are most important for the base mechanics analysis, and what role does each play?
questions.instructor: The four wires are deformable axial members and control vertical displacement. Rigid members AB and DC distribute forces and impose displacement compatibility but are assumed not to deform.

questions.title: Mechanical Response and Scope
learningObjectives: Identify the responses supported by the supplied data.
questions.student: Identify the mechanical responses considered for the wires and rigid members in this problem.
questions.instructor: The wires undergo axial tension and elongation. The rigid members undergo small vertical translations and rotations produced by unequal endpoint displacements. Strength failure, fatigue, connector stress, and rigid-member bending are outside the base problem.

questions.title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Connect the input variables to equilibrium and axial deformation.
questions.student: Identify the loading, geometric, and material parameters that control displacement and tilt.
questions.instructor: The required inputs are P, Aw, Ew, Lu, Ll, LDC, LAB, xDH, and xP. The remaining upper span is xHC = LDC - xDH = {{platform_x_HC_ft}} ft.

questions.title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Convert the real assembly into two rigid bodies connected by axial wires.
questions.student: Before using the reference figure, draw a simplified Mechanics of Materials model. Show the fixed anchors, four vertical wires, rigid members AB and DC, payload location, and symbolic dimensions. Include separate free-body diagrams for both rigid members.
questions.instructor: A correct model has two horizontal rigid members connected by vertical axial tension wires. The upper member is suspended from fixed anchors by ED and FC; the lower member is suspended from the upper member by AH and BC; and concentrated load P acts eccentrically on AB.
questions.gradingNotes: Students should attempt the model before seeing the instructor reference idealization.

questions.title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting equilibrium and compatibility analysis.
questions.student: State the assumptions used to convert the physical system into the simplified mechanics model.
questions.instructor: Typical assumptions are rigid members AB and DC; straight, vertical, uniform, linearly elastic wires; axial wire force only; fixed anchors E and F; static loading; small displacement and rotation; ideal pin or eye connections; and neglected wire self-weight and local connection effects.

questions.title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the coupled equilibrium and displacement solution.
questions.student: Before calculating, describe the analysis sequence needed to determine load displacement and member tilt.
questions.instructor: Use equilibrium of AB to find lower-wire forces; use equilibrium of DC to find upper-wire forces; calculate all four wire elongations; interpolate the upper-member displacement at H; add lower-wire elongations to obtain displacements at A and B; interpolate at the load point; then calculate each member's small-angle rotation from its endpoint displacement difference.

questions.title: Boundary Conditions and Unknown Wire Forces
learningObjectives: Interpret the reference idealization and define unknown tensions.
questions.student: From the instructor reference diagram, identify the fixed points, rigid bodies, and four unknown wire forces.
questions.instructor: Ceiling anchors E and F are fixed. AB and DC are rigid bodies. The unknown axial tensions are TED, TFC, TAH, and TBC, each acting vertically along its wire.

questions.title: Equilibrium of Lower Member AB
learningObjectives: Determine lower-wire forces under eccentric loading.
questions.student: Draw the free-body diagram of lower member AB. For P = {{P}} {{P_unit}}, LAB = {{L_AB}} {{L_AB_unit}}, and xP = {{x_P}} {{x_P_unit}}, determine TAH and TBC.
questions.instructor: For AB, ΣFy = 0 gives TAH + TBC = P. Moments about A give TBCLAB = PxP. Therefore TBC = {{platform_T_BC_lb}} lb and TAH = {{platform_T_AH_lb}} lb.
questions.commonMistakes: The eccentric load does not split equally between the lower wires.

questions.title: Equilibrium of Upper Member DC
learningObjectives: Transfer lower-wire forces to the upper rigid member and solve support tensions.
questions.student: Draw the free-body diagram of upper member DC and determine TED and TFC. Show where the lower-wire forces act on DC.
questions.instructor: The lower wires apply downward forces TAH at H and TBC at C. Thus TED + TFC = P. Moments about D give TFCLDC = TAHxDH + TBCLDC. Therefore TFC = {{platform_T_FC_lb}} lb and TED = {{platform_T_ED_lb}} lb.

questions.title: Wire Elongations
learningObjectives: Calculate elongation of all four tension wires with consistent units.
questions.student: Calculate the elongation of each wire using δ = FL/(AE). Use Aw = {{A_w}} {{A_w_unit}} and Ew = {{E_w}} {{E_w_unit}}.
questions.instructor:
Use Lu = {{L_u}} ft = {{L_u}}(12) in, Ll = {{L_l}} ft = {{L_l}}(12) in, and Ew = {{E_w}} ksi = {{E_w}}(1000) psi.

δAH = {{platform_delta_AH_in}} in, δBC = {{platform_delta_BC_in}} in, δED = {{platform_delta_ED_in}} in, and δFC = {{platform_delta_FC_in}} in.
questions.commonMistakes: Convert feet to inches and ksi to psi when force is in pounds and area is in square inches.

questions.title: Displacement of Point H
learningObjectives: Interpolate displacement along a rigid member undergoing small rotation.
questions.student: Using rigid-body compatibility of upper member DC, determine the downward displacement of point H.
questions.instructor:
Point D moves downward by δED, and C moves downward by δFC. Since H is xDH/LDC of the distance from D to C,

δH = δD + (δC - δD)(xDH/LDC) = {{platform_delta_H_in}} in downward.

questions.title: Endpoint Displacements of Lower Member AB
learningObjectives: Combine support motion and lower-wire elongation.
questions.student: Determine the downward displacements of endpoints A and B of lower rigid member AB.
questions.instructor: Point A is suspended from moving point H through wire AH, so δA = δH + δAH = {{platform_delta_A_in}} in downward. Point B is suspended from moving point C through wire BC, so δB = δC + δBC = {{platform_delta_B_in}} in downward.
questions.gradingNotes: Both upper-support motion and lower-wire elongation must be included.

questions.title: Vertical Displacement of the Equipment Load
learningObjectives: Determine load-point displacement from endpoint motions.
questions.student: Determine the vertical displacement of the equipment load on lower member AB.
questions.instructor: The load is xP/LAB of the distance from A to B. Therefore δload = δA + (δB - δA)(xP/LAB) = {{platform_delta_load_in}} in downward.

questions.title: Tilt of Lower Member AB
learningObjectives: Calculate and interpret the small-angle rotation of AB.
questions.student: Determine the small-angle tilt magnitude and physical direction of lower member AB.
questions.instructor: |θAB| ≈ |δB - δA|/LAB = {{platform_theta_AB_rad}} rad = {{platform_theta_AB_deg}}°. Member AB tilts {{platform_lower_tilt_direction}}.

questions.title: Tilt of Upper Member DC
learningObjectives: Calculate and interpret the small-angle rotation of DC.
questions.student: Determine the small-angle tilt magnitude and physical direction of upper member DC.
questions.instructor: |θDC| ≈ |δC - δD|/LDC = {{platform_theta_DC_rad}} rad = {{platform_theta_DC_deg}}°. Member DC tilts {{platform_upper_tilt_direction}}.

questions.title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Interpret the mechanics results and make a limited recommendation.
questions.student: Identify the wire carrying the largest force and the largest elongation. Use the results to recommend one change that would reduce load displacement or tilt, and state what additional information is needed before service approval.
questions.instructor: Wire {{platform_governing_wire}} carries the largest force, {{platform_governing_force_lb}} lb. Wire {{platform_dominant_wire}} has the largest elongation, {{platform_dominant_elongation_in}} in. The predicted payload displacement is {{platform_delta_load_in}} in downward. Increasing wire area or modulus reduces all wire elongations; reducing load eccentricity especially reduces unequal lower-wire elongation and lower-member tilt. Service approval also requires allowable stresses, fatigue requirements, anchor and connector geometry, rigid-member stiffness, tolerances, and applicable facility criteria.
questions.gradingNotes: The recommendation must remain within this deformation model and must not claim that strength or durability has been verified.

title: Torsional Response of a Multi-Stage Turbine Rotor
summary: A turbine-rotor torsion problem integrating a linearly varying internal-torque function, reaction torque, polar moment, angle-of-twist integration, maximum shear stress, and parameter sensitivity.
idealizedImageAlt: Instructor reference idealization of a turbine rotor with torque-free journal bearings at A and B, a fixed section at C, section D, and a linearly varying blade-region torque model.
problemStatement:
A power-generation engineering team is evaluating a uniform solid turbine rotor. Successive blade stages transfer torque into the shaft over the active region C-D, so the cumulative internal torque changes continuously along that region.

For this assignment, the stated linear quantity is the internal torque resultant T(x) = TDx/L, not a torque intensity per unit length. Journal bearings A and B are torque-free, while section C is fixed in rotation.
engineeringGoal: Derive the internal-torque function, determine the relative angle of twist at D and the absolute maximum torsional shear stress, identify the governing location, and explain the parameters controlling strength and stiffness.

variables.label: Loaded blade-region length C to D

questions.title: Primary Function of the Rotor Shaft
learningObjectives: Identify the rotor shaft's role in the turbine system.
questions.student: State the primary structural and mechanical function of the rotor shaft.
questions.instructor: The rotor shaft transmits torque from the turbine stages to the connected drivetrain while maintaining acceptable torsional strength and stiffness.

questions.title: Blade-Generated Torsional Loading
learningObjectives: Connect blade loading to a varying internal torque.
questions.student: Explain how the turbine blade stages load the shaft in the base model.
questions.instructor: The blade stages apply torque about the shaft axis. Their cumulative effect makes the internal torque resultant vary continuously along C-D rather than remain constant between isolated point loads.

questions.title: Supports and Rotational Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Distinguish radial support from rotational restraint.
questions.student: Identify supports A, B, and C and state what each prevents.
questions.instructor: Journal bearings A and B prevent radial translation but allow shaft-axis rotation, so they provide no torsional reaction in the ideal model. Section C is fixed against rotation, so θ(C) = 0 and a reaction torque develops there.

questions.title: Torsional Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace torque transfer from the blades to the restraint.
questions.student: Trace the torsional load path through the turbine rotor.
questions.instructor: Steam forces act on the blades; blade hubs transfer torque into the rotor; the shaft carries cumulative internal torque toward restrained section C; and the fixed connection supplies the balancing reaction torque.

questions.title: Expected Critical Location
learningObjectives: Predict the location of maximum torsional stress.
questions.student: Before calculating, predict where the maximum torsional shear stress will occur and explain why.
questions.instructor: Maximum stress occurs where the magnitude of internal torque is largest and at the shaft's outer surface. For the stated linear internal-torque model, the critical cross section is D.

questions.title: Governing Mechanical Responses
learningObjectives: Identify the responses included in the base problem.
questions.student: Identify the mechanical responses central to this problem and list important responses outside the base model.
questions.instructor: The base responses are torsional strength, represented by maximum shear stress, and torsional stiffness, represented by relative angle of twist. Bearing stresses, blade stresses, bending, fatigue, vibration, and thermal behavior are outside the base model.

questions.title: Key Geometry and Material Parameters
learningObjectives: Explain how diameter, length, and modulus affect torsional response.
questions.student: Identify the key geometric and material parameters and describe how they affect stress or twist.
questions.instructor: Shaft diameter d controls J proportional to d4, twist proportional to 1/d4, and stress proportional to 1/d3. Loaded length L affects twist linearly. Shear modulus G affects twist but not elastic stress for prescribed torque.

questions.title: Student-Generated Turbine-Shaft Idealization
learningObjectives: Create a varying-torque shaft model before viewing the reference figure.
questions.student: Before using the reference figure, create a simplified shaft model showing A, B, fixed section C, section D, coordinate x measured from C, and the linearly varying internal torque T(x). Include a circular cross section with diameter d.
questions.instructor: A valid model shows a prismatic circular shaft with θ(C) = 0, ideal torque-free journal bearings at A and B, and T(x) = TDx/L for 0 ≤ x ≤ L.
questions.gradingNotes: Students should attempt the model before seeing the instructor idealization.

questions.title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the turbine-shaft model.
questions.student: State the assumptions required for the base mechanics model.
questions.instructor: Assume a uniform solid circular shaft, homogeneous isotropic linear-elastic material, Saint-Venant torsion, small twist, constant G and d, ideal bearings that transmit no shaft-axis torque, and a perfectly fixed section C. Neglect blade size, local stress concentrations, bending, dynamics, thermal effects, and fatigue.

questions.title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan a complete varying-torque analysis.
questions.student: Outline the calculation sequence before substituting numbers.
questions.instructor: Define T(x); determine the reaction torque at C; construct the internal-torque diagram; compute J; integrate T(x)/(JG) for twist; evaluate Tc/J for stress; and interpret the governing section and parameter sensitivity.

questions.title: Torsional Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: State the boundary conditions used in the torsion solution.
questions.student: State the torsional boundary conditions at A, B, and C.
questions.instructor: At fixed section C, θ(C) = 0. Ideal journal bearings A and B permit rotation and supply no reaction torque about the shaft axis. Their radial reactions are outside the torsion-only model.

questions.title: Fixed-Section Reaction Torque
learningObjectives: Determine the balancing torsional reaction.
questions.student: Identify the unknown torsional reaction at C and determine its magnitude and sense.
questions.instructor: The fixed section supplies a reaction torque of magnitude {{turbine_reaction_lbft}} lb·ft, opposite the sense of the blade-region torque. Bearings A and B supply no shaft-axis reaction torque.

questions.title: Internal Torque Function and Diagram
learningObjectives: Define and graph a linearly varying internal torque resultant.
questions.student: Define the internal torque along C-D and construct its diagram. Clearly distinguish an internal torque resultant from a torque intensity per unit length.
questions.instructor:
With x measured from C, T(x) = TDx/L for 0 ≤ x ≤ L. The diagram is triangular, increasing from zero at C to TD at D. The area-average internal torque is {{turbine_average_torque_lbft}} lb·ft.

Here T(x) has torque units; it is not a distributed intensity w(x) with torque-per-length units.
questions.commonMistakes: Do not integrate the stated T(x) once more as though it were a torque intensity.

questions.title: Polar Moment of Inertia
learningObjectives: Calculate the polar moment for a solid circular shaft.
questions.student: Determine the polar moment of inertia J for the assigned solid shaft.
questions.instructor: J = πd4/32 = {{turbine_J_in4}} in4.

questions.title: Relative Angle of Twist at D
learningObjectives: Integrate a varying internal torque to determine twist.
questions.student: Determine the angle of twist at D relative to C. Show the integral and use consistent inch-pound units.
questions.instructor:
φD/C = ∫0L T(x)/(JG) dx = TDL/(2JG).

Using L = {{turbine_L_in}} in and TD = {{turbine_T_D_lbin}} lb·in, φD/C = {{turbine_phi_rad}} rad = {{turbine_phi_deg}}°.

questions.title: Absolute Maximum Torsional Shear Stress
learningObjectives: Calculate maximum shaft stress and locate it physically.
questions.student: Determine the absolute maximum torsional shear stress and identify its location.
questions.instructor: The largest |T| occurs at D. Therefore τmax = TD(d/2)/J = {{turbine_tau_psi}} psi = {{turbine_tau_ksi}} ksi. It occurs at the outer surface of section D.

questions.title: Torsional Sensitivity
learningObjectives: Compare how design variables affect stress and twist.
questions.student: Explain which design variable most effectively reduces both twist and stress. Compare the effects of increasing diameter, increasing shear modulus, and reducing loaded length.
questions.instructor: Increasing diameter is most effective because J scales with d4, twist scales with 1/d4, and maximum stress scales with 1/d3. Increasing G reduces twist but not stress for prescribed torque. Reducing L reduces twist but not maximum stress at D.

questions.title: Engineering Assessment
learningObjectives: Make a bounded recommendation from the torsion results.
questions.student: Provide a limited engineering recommendation based on the torsion model and identify the checks needed before final turbine-shaft approval.
questions.instructor:
{{turbine_recommendation}}

Final design must verify the intended loading interpretation and include bending, combined stress, fatigue, stress concentrations, blade and rotor dynamics, vibration, thermal gradients, bearings, and project-specific stress and twist limits.
questions.gradingNotes: Students should not claim full rotor safety without allowable limits and the omitted coupled analyses.

title: Torsional Stiffness of a Variable-Radius Aluminum Drive Shaft
summary: A nonprismatic-shaft torsion problem integrating a variable polar moment, numerical angle-of-twist integration, maximum shear stress, compliance localization, and stiffness assessment.
idealizedImageAlt: Instructor reference idealization of a solid tapered shaft with applied torque at end A, fixed support at the large end, coordinate x, length L, and variable radius r of x.
problemStatement:
A mechanical engineering team is evaluating a lightweight 2014-T6 aluminum torque-transmission shaft for a precision industrial drive or test system. The solid shaft radius increases continuously from the torque-input end A toward a rigid mounting interface.

To keep the radius law dimensionally consistent, define ξ = x/(1 m) and use r(x) = r0[1 + ξ3/2 + ξ5/2]. The shaft carries constant internal torque but has a position-dependent polar moment.
engineeringGoal: Determine the angular rotation of end A relative to the fixed interface, locate the maximum torsional shear stress, quantify where torsional compliance accumulates, and assess the shaft against the assigned twist limit.

questions.title: Primary Function of the Tapered Shaft
learningObjectives: Identify the shaft's role in the drive or test system.
questions.student: State the primary mechanical function of the tapered shaft.
questions.instructor: The shaft transmits torque between the input coupling and the fixed or driven machine interface while limiting rotational compliance.

questions.title: External Torsional Loading
learningObjectives: Identify the load entering the shaft.
questions.student: Identify the externally applied mechanical load and where it enters the system.
questions.instructor: A shaft-axis torque T is applied at end A through the input coupling.

questions.title: Fixed-End Boundary Condition
learningObjectives: State the rotational restraint at the large end.
questions.student: Identify the torsional boundary condition at the large end and explain its mechanical consequence.
questions.instructor: The large end is fixed against rotation, so its angular displacement is zero and the interface develops a reaction torque.

questions.title: Torque Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace torque transfer from input to support.
questions.student: Trace the torque load path from the input coupling to the support.
questions.instructor: The path is input coupling, small-radius end A, continuously varying shaft, fixed interface, and machine frame.

questions.title: Expected Compliance-Dominating Region
learningObjectives: Predict where most shaft twist will accumulate.
questions.student: Before calculating, identify the shaft region expected to contribute most strongly to total twist and explain why.
questions.instructor: The small-radius region near A should dominate because J is proportional to r4 and local torsional compliance is proportional to 1/r4.

questions.title: Parameters Governing Twist
learningObjectives: Identify inputs controlling the angle of twist.
questions.student: Identify the geometric, loading, and material parameters governing the angle of twist.
questions.instructor: The governing parameters are applied torque T, shaft length L, radius function r(x), and shear modulus G.

questions.title: Why Integration Is Required
learningObjectives: Explain why a constant-section twist formula is insufficient.
questions.student: Explain why the constant-section equation φ = TL/(JG) cannot be used directly.
questions.instructor: The radius and polar moment vary with position, so local differential twist must be integrated along the shaft. No single constant J represents the actual geometry.

questions.title: Student-Generated Tapered-Shaft Idealization
learningObjectives: Create a variable-radius torsion model before viewing the reference figure.
questions.student: Before using the reference figure, draw a solid circular shaft of length L with coordinate x measured from end A, applied torque T at A, and zero rotation at the opposite end. Label r(x), J(x), and the internal torque.
questions.instructor: A valid model shows a solid nonprismatic circular shaft carrying constant internal torque, with x measured from A and zero rotation at the fixed large end.
questions.gradingNotes: Students should attempt the idealization before seeing the instructor reference figure.

questions.title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the nonprismatic torsion model.
questions.student: State the assumptions needed for the base torsion model.
questions.instructor: Assume Saint-Venant torsion of a solid circular shaft, homogeneous isotropic linear-elastic material, constant G, small rotation, and torque applied about the shaft axis. Neglect bending, axial loading, local stress concentrations, attachment flexibility, and warping effects.

questions.title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan a complete nonprismatic-shaft analysis.
questions.student: Write the calculation sequence before substituting values.
questions.instructor: Determine the reaction and internal torque; define the nondimensional coordinate and radius law; write J(x) = πr(x)4/2; use dφ = T dx/[GJ(x)]; integrate from 0 to L; calculate stress; and interpret the result.

questions.title: Boundary Condition and Reaction Torque
learningObjectives: Determine the fixed-end torsional reaction.
questions.student: State the fixed-end rotational boundary condition and determine the reaction torque.
questions.instructor: The fixed-end rotation is zero. Static equilibrium gives a reaction torque of magnitude {{taper_reaction_Nm}} N·m, opposite the applied torque.

questions.title: Internal Torque Distribution
learningObjectives: Determine internal torque throughout the shaft.
questions.student: Determine the internal torque Tint(x) for 0 ≤ x ≤ L.
questions.instructor: Because no additional torques act along the shaft, Tint(x) = T throughout 0 ≤ x ≤ L.

questions.title: Radius Function and Variable Polar Moment
learningObjectives: Write a dimensionally consistent radius law and variable polar moment.
questions.student: Define a dimensionally consistent radius function and write the polar moment of inertia as a function of position.
questions.instructor:
Define ξ = x/(1 m). Then r(x) = r0[1 + ξ3/2 + ξ5/2] and J(x) = πr(x)4/2.

For the assigned geometry, r(0) = {{taper_r_A_m}} m, r(L) = {{taper_r_L_m}} m, and J(0) = {{taper_J_A_m4}} m4.

questions.title: Differential Twist Relation
learningObjectives: Derive the local twist relation for the tapered shaft.
questions.student: Write the differential relation for shaft rotation in terms of T, G, and r(x).
questions.instructor: dφ = T dx/[GJ(x)] = 2T dx/[πG r(x)4].

questions.title: Angle-of-Twist Integral
learningObjectives: Formulate the total rotation integral.
questions.student: Formulate the definite integral for rotation of end A relative to the fixed end.
questions.instructor: φA = ∫0L 2T/[πG r(x)4] dx. The evaluated geometric integral ∫0L dx/r(x)4 is {{taper_integral_m_neg3}} m-3.

questions.title: Numerical Angle of Twist
learningObjectives: Numerically evaluate the nonprismatic-shaft twist.
questions.student: Evaluate the twist integral numerically and report the angle in radians and degrees.
questions.instructor: Using G = {{taper_G_Pa}} Pa, φA = {{taper_phi_rad}} rad = {{taper_phi_deg}}°.
questions.gradingNotes: Numerical quadrature, a documented calculator integral, or equivalent computational evaluation is acceptable.

questions.title: Maximum Torsional Shear Stress
learningObjectives: Calculate and locate the maximum stress in a tapered shaft.
questions.student: Determine the maximum torsional shear stress and identify its location.
questions.instructor: τmax(x) = 2T/[πr(x)3]. Because the radius is smallest at x = 0, the maximum occurs at the outer surface of end A: {{taper_tau_max_MPa}} MPa.

questions.title: Compliance Localization and Sensitivity
learningObjectives: Explain why the small-end region controls twist and stress.
questions.student: Explain why a modest increase in minimum radius can strongly reduce both stress and twist. Quantify how much of the assigned total twist accumulates in the first quarter of the shaft.
questions.instructor: Stress varies as 1/r3 and the twist integrand as 1/r4, so the minimum-radius region has disproportionate influence. For the assigned profile, approximately {{taper_first_quarter_pct}}% of the total twist accumulates over 0 ≤ x ≤ L/4.

questions.title: Stiffness Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Assess torsional stiffness and recommend a modification.
questions.student: Compare the calculated rotation with the assigned allowable twist and make a limited mechanics-based recommendation.
questions.instructor:
The twist utilization is {{taper_twist_utilization}}. {{taper_twist_assessment}}

{{taper_recommendation}}

Detailed design must also consider strength allowables, bending, attachment flexibility, stress concentrations, fatigue, dynamics, manufacturing limits, and applicable standards.
